title: Iowa announces Nebraska game is sold out
summary: The Iowa athletic department has announced that the Black Friday game against Nebraska is sold out.
content: The Iowa Athletics Department has announced that Friday's Pioneer Heroes Game against Nebraska at Kinnick Stadium is sold out . The game kicks off at 11 a.m. CT and will be televised on CBS. Iowa (9-2, 6-2) has sold out 35 consecutive games at Kinnick Stadium, dating back to the start of the 2022 season. Nebraska (7-4, 4-4) has a home sellout streak that currently stands at 417 consecutive games. Nebraska is coming off a 31-28 victory over Ohio State last Saturday in Lincoln. The victory was the Huskers' first over a ranked opponent since 2016 (35-31 win against No. 22 Oregon ). Iowa enters Friday's game following a 34-17 win at Illinois last weekend. The Hawkeyes are on a four-game winning streak and are still in the running for a spot in the Big Ten Championship Game. The Hawkeyes were ranked 15th in last week's College Football Playoff rankings and are still in the running for a spot in the final Big Ten Championship Game. Iowa has appeared in the title game three times (2015, 2021, 2023) and is 0-3 as a program. Friday's game is the 57th all-time meeting between these two schools and the 16th meeting as Big Ten Conference opponents. Nebraska leads the series 30-23-3 all-time but Iowa has an 11-4 series lead as Big Ten opponents. title: John Mateer’s legacy with OU football is his mental, physical toughness
summary: John Mateer could’ve easily sat out the rest of the season when his most-influential mentor got fired during the campaign. However, through his struggles with turnovers and winning football games, Mateer persevered and is playing his best down the stretch of his final college games the past month — cementing his weird, but empowering legacy in Norman. Mateer, Oklahoma football’s starting ...
content: John Mateer could’ve easily sat out the rest of the season when his most-influential mentor got fired during the campaign. However, through his struggles with turnovers and winning football games, Mateer persevered and is playing his best down the stretch of his final college games the past month — cementing his weird, but empowering legacy in Norman. Mateer, Oklahoma football’s starting quarterback, is playing his final regular-season college football game Saturday when the Sooners take on No. 23 Missouri in Columbia, Missouri, at 3:15 p.m. on SEC Network. His legacy as OU’s starting quarterback is not to the level that Sooner fans are quite used to, however he’s fought through a broken throwing hand, turnover mistakes and a coordinator change. Through all of that, though, he’s finally playing his best football throughout the past three weeks, getting the designation as the Southeastern Conference’s Offensive Player of the Week for his performance against Texas A&M last week. He ended his Owen Field career with a somersaulting touchdown run on 4th-and-7 that put the 28-7 win in the bag for the Sooners, and gave Mateer an incredible last play in Norman. “That was obviously a fun play. I was getting in the end zone somehow, I didn’t realize I’d be upside down,” Mateer said. “It was fun. You soak it in. We’ve got a game to win, but I think the two-minute timeout in the fourth quarter was a good opportunity for me to really soak it in. I was looking around. It’s a beautiful place to play and has so much history. I’m just honored for the opportunity to play here.” Mateer has been usually the hottest topic in Norman since his arrival. Multiple media scrums a week, plenty of sometimes warranted criticism and a few bad performances in his time with the Sooners. However, his mental toughness has prevailed through it all — the good and the bad — and it’s the most impressive thing he’s done for his coach, OU coach Brent Venables. “What a great example of a guy that has tightened his jaw and has decided to be better and focus on things that he can control and to not let the opinions of others put him in a bad place,” Venables said. “I think he’s a great example for somebody in this arena that fails in front of the world, and it’s easy to cast stones and make assumptions and label a guy this or that. And it just comes with it. “Everybody certainly has the opportunity to get better, and he’s chosen to do that, which is admirable, and obviously, when he’s doing well, our team does well.” Before Mateer ended his Owen Field career upside down in the end zone, he received the highest honor an OU football player could receive. Mateer, along with Peyton Bowen, Taylor Wein and Owen Heinecke, were recognized prior to Saturday’s game as the 2026 Don Key Award winners. The Don Key Award is given annually to one or more OU football players that best exemplifies the many superior qualities of former OU football player Don Key, both on the field and in the classroom. Key was a three-year starter and potential All-American for the Sooners before cancer surgery ended his football career in 1981. The award is renowned and well-respected amongst the OU faithful, and for Mateer to earn that honor after everything he’s been through with the Sooners is fitting in Venables’ eyes. “That was cool for him to be able to be recognized last weekend as one of the Don Key Award recipients. Really, really cool,” Venables said. “I think that embodies really what he’s meant to our locker room here the last two years. I’m happy for him. He’s worked incredibly hard. He’s gone through a lot of tough moments here along the way. Learned a lot, probably about himself and just kind of life, and then again the game of football. “But again, he’s hung in there, and he’s made the best of it. Proud of it.” Venables made the hard decision earlier this season to get rid of Mateer’s biggest influence in former offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle. Arbuckle was fired Oct. 31 after OU’s 42-25 loss to South Carolina, which effectively ended the Sooners’ chances at a College Football Playoff repeat appearance. Mateer and Arbuckle were together for nearly four years — two in Norman and two at Washington State. Mateer ran Arbuckle’s system for three years and it’s what got them both to Norman, however it ended the way neither of them wanted it to end. Mateer could’ve easily been done with the season and his college career, he was struggling mightily with turnover and accuracy issues. However, he dug in and collabed with interim coordinator Jason Witten and has since played his best football since arriving in Norman. He’s been consistent in running the football effectively, mostly keeping the football protected and is making better and more accurate decisions in his throws. Mateer has found his groove in recent weeks and never wavered in his belief in himself, which is why he’s always had the respect of his team. It’s why the Sooners stayed with him as their starter when he was struggling, when it could’ve been easy to hand the ball over to someone else. It’s why Venables said he’s got the utmost respect for Mateer and how he’s handled himself through the trials and tribulations this season. “Nobody in that space stopped believing in him. I think that’s important. It gives him the fuel that sometimes you need to pull you through the knot hole,” Venables said. “I think he’s done a really good job from a maturation standpoint of just again putting himself in a quiet place. Not an easy thing to do in the world that they all live in, and certainly being in a place like Oklahoma. “He’d be the first one to tell you there’s nothing easy about it. Just like having success, there’s nothing easy about handling the success, but he’s been a great example of how to navigate some real choppy waters.”

title: Lance Jackson, Colton Vasek have stepped up after injury to Colin Simmons
summary: The Texas defense has continued to play at a high level after the injury to its star edge rusher thanks to other players emerging.
content: AUSTIN, TX - OCTOBER 17: Texas Longhorns edge Lance Jackson #40 celebrates a stop on third down late in the SEC football game between the Texas Longhorns and Florida Gators on October 17, 2026, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images AUSTIN — No Colin Simmons, no problem? It’s not exactly that simple for the Texas Longhorns heading into Friday’s regular-season finale against the Texas A&M Aggies, for which the standout edge rusher was listed as questionable on the first two initial SEC-mandated player availability reports. Simmons has been able to play two games since suffering a high ankle sprain in last month’s loss to Florida, and Texas still unquestionably misses his speed off the edge and improved ability to defend the run, but in addition to senior linebacker Rasheem Biles making an impact as a blitzer, sophomore edge Lance Jackson and senior edge Colton Vasek have both stepped up for the Longhorns in recent games, allowing Texas to maintain its elite defense. While Jackson and Vasek are both making a difference, their respective journeys to this point have looked quite different. A consensus five-star prospect out of Texarkana Pleasant Grove, Jackson finished the 2025 recruiting cycle as the nation’s No. 21 prospect and the No. 2 edge, according to the 247Sports Composite rankings, following a senior season during which he recorded nine sacks and 28.5 tackles for loss. For a prospect of Jackson’s caliber, any drama in his recruitment was remarkably absent — despite holding close to 30 offers from top programs, the 6’5, 274-pounder visited Austin for a Junior Day in early 2024 and committed one day later, then stayed true to Texas until he signed. After showing promise as a freshman, playing 261 snaps and recording 16 tackles and two sacks, Jackson has emerged as an impact defender this season in what Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian termed a “phenomenal season.” “We’re asking this guy to do a lot of different things. He’s playing multiple positions. He’s doing it at a really high level. Had a big-time sack fumble Saturday. He’s the lead against the run. His effort is tremendous, and what I love about Lance is he plays with an edge. He plays with a real edge and he sets the tone for how we want our guys to play,” Sarkisian said. Jackson’s combination of size, length, and mass enable him to all the way from three technique to everything outside as far as a nine technique. Against Ole Miss, defensive coordinator Will Muschamp often employed him in coverage, too, a role in which Jackson has only allowed four catches for 29 yards. Early in the season, Jackson was putting himself in position to make plays, but was struggling to finish them with six missed tackles over the first six games. Since then, his growth has resulted in fewer mistakes and more big-time plays. The alignment versatility for Jackson showed up against Missouri with his ability to wreck the preferred outside zone scheme employed by the Tigers. That’s physicality, holmes. Lance Jackson has become a hell of a player. @ontexasfootball pic.twitter.com/OYkW99DhLh — CJ Vogel (@CJVogel_OTF) November 9, 2026 In the blowout win over Arkansas, Jackson played the best game of his career, earning an astounding 94.9 overall grade from Pro Football Focus by recording five total pressures, including that sack fumble, four tackles, and three defensive stops. No other Power Four edge graded out higher than Jackson last week . Excellent setting up end-tackle twists because of his strength crashing inside, Jackson uses the threat of his inside moves to maximize his danger off the edge. He doesn’t have the pure explosiveness of Simmons — that’s a physics problem as much as anything — but he moves exceptionally well for his size. When the Arkansas right tackle got too flat on his pass set worrying about an inside move, Jackson’s ball get off and length combined to get the tackle out over his toes, allowing him to easily take the edge and force the fumble. Lance Jackson pass rush win. Improvements are showing up every single week. pic.twitter.com/eQeNe9Dbfo — CJ Vogel (@CJVogel_OTF) November 23, 2026 The concern about Jackson’s inside moves is a result of his impressive lateral quickness that allows him to win across the face of offensive tackles. Texas DE Lance Jackson had the Arkansas right tackle (and quarterback) in hell all day. pic.twitter.com/qBLPrqKbwN — Tyler Horka (@tbhorka) November 24, 2026 Those are the ways in which Jackson’s physical attributes show up on the field — he’s good enough off the edge to force opponents to use a tight end to chip him, but even that tactic can’t account for how his motor amplifies his athleticism. 6-foot-6, 275 pounds moving like this… Special athlete here https://t.co/hJCbfuDYxX pic.twitter.com/n6ozAhKOV9 — CJ Vogel (@CJVogel_OTF) November 23, 2026 Jackson’s intensity, the fuel for his motor, sometimes runs too hot — Sarkisian also addressed the five penalties Jackson has committed this season, the most on the team defensively, noting that he would rather have to pull back on his hard-nosed young defender than to find ways to get his motor to fire. It fires and it misfires. “I wouldn’t change it for the world — I think that what he provides for us is irreplaceable that way,” Sarkisian said. It’s an issue further maturity should solve. And, in any case, those moments do not obscure the incredible ceiling that Jackson possesses as a potential future first-round pick. Less than two years into his Texas career, Jackson is on the right trajectory to reach that ceiling. The Longhorns defense is also benefitting from the long-awaited breakout season by senior defensive end Colton Vasek, a Texas legacy from Austin Westlake whose high-profile flip from Oklahoma during the 2023 recruiting class elevated his profile beyond his ranking as a fringe top-100 prospect. Added to the program at a time when the Horns were desperately seeking edge-rushing talent, Vasek’s career was derailed by injuries over his first three seasons. “For Colton, I couldn’t be happier. You’re always happy for guys on your team, and everybody’s journey is different. Colton’s had a tough road with the multitude of injuries that he’s gone through,” Sarkisian said. As a freshman, Vasek redshirted after suffering a back injury. In 2024, hip and shoulder injuries limited Vasek to 65 snaps over 11 games and led to offseason surgery to repair a torn labrum. Despite the surgery, Vasek continued playing with a harness on his shoulder in 2025, when his playing time doubled, but he only made three tackles. Passed by younger players on the depth chart, Vasek only projected as a special teams contributor in 2026. Instead, he’s found an increasingly important role since Simmons was injured, averaging 22 snaps per game during the five-game Texas winning streak, recording 16 of his 23 tackles with three tackles for loss and two sacks. “For him to be able to be healthy this year and be a real contributor for us, not only on defense but on special teams, it’s awesome. I’m really happy for him, and he serves as such a great model for other guys in the program who are going through injuries or different setbacks along the way — look at 92, man. Look at what he’s been through, and look at how he’s contributing to the team now,” Sarkisian said. One of Vasek’s sacks came at a big moment in the Missouri game — tied at 20-20 in the fourth quarter and backed up in their own territory, the 6’5, 252-pounder pinned the Tigers at their own goal line by dropping Austin Simmons for a 10-yard loss. COLTON VASEK WITH A HUGE SACK pic.twitter.com/kV7vbkhJnO — Nash (@NashTalksTexas) November 7, 2026 As a run defender, Vasek can make opponents pay for leaving him unblocked on the back side. Dare I say who I thought this reminded me of when I saw it live… What a 2nd half of the season Colton Vasek is having for #Texas . pic.twitter.com/7BKaY2h3Ey — CJ Vogel (@CJVogel_OTF) November 24, 2026 Notice Jackson playing the 4i there. Vasek also been effective in coverage. In 23 coverage snaps this season, the Austin Westlake product has only allowed three catches for nine yards. One of his best plays in coverage won’t show up in the box score — anticipating a Texas tendency, Missouri isolated Vasek against running back Jamal Roberts on a wheel route, the type of play a good offensive coordinator schemes up during the week and waits for the right time to call. But instead of producing an explosive, potentially game-changing play, Vasek played his assignment, took the right angle, and had enough juice to run with Roberts down the field, forcing Simmons off that read. And Vasek still remains a core contributor on special teams, reprising the role he’s played over the last several seasons — with 195 snaps over four units, only Ryan Niblett has been on the field for more snaps on special teams than Vasek. “He blocked a field goal or gets his hand on a field goal two weeks ago,” Sarkisian said. “He’s on punt protection. He’s on kickoff return, so his role on the team has elevated, and I couldn’t be happier for anybody on the team than for Vasek because I know what he’s been through to get to this point.”

title: Lane Kiffin Forced to Address Controversial On-Air Moment as LSU Frustrations Boil Over
summary: BATON ROUGE, La. — LSU football coach Lane Kiffin is no stranger to controversy, but his latest public remarks created an uncomfortable moment for the Tigers’ own broadcasting crew. Kiffin addressed the incident during his weekly news conference Monday, apologizing for an emotional outburst that aired on the LSU Sports Radio Network during Saturday’s 27-13 loss to Tennessee. The apology followed the circulation of a…
content: Nov 21, 2026; Knoxville, Tennessee, USA; Louisiana State head coach Lane Kiffin reacts after a play against the Tennessee Volunteers during the second half at Neyland Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Randy Sartin-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters) BATON ROUGE, La. — LSU football coach Lane Kiffin is no stranger to controversy, but his latest public remarks created an uncomfortable moment for the Tigers’ own broadcasting crew. Kiffin addressed the incident during his weekly news conference Monday, apologizing for an emotional outburst that aired on the LSU Sports Radio Network during Saturday’s 27-13 loss to Tennessee. The apology followed the circulation of a video showing the reaction of LSU’s radio announcers, who appeared caught off guard by the coach’s language. Kiffin’s Remarks Leave LSU Radio Booth Stunned The incident occurred during Kiffin’s halftime interview with LSU sideline reporter Gordy Rush at Neyland Stadium. LSU trailed Tennessee 10-6 after a controversial targeting penalty against Tigers safety Ty Benefield helped the Volunteers score a touchdown shortly before halftime. Kiffin initially discussed LSU’s offensive struggles before using two profanities to criticize the targeting decision. The remarks immediately created an awkward situation for LSU’s broadcast team. Video from the radio booth showed play-by-play announcer Chris Blair removing his headset and putting his head in his hands. Analyst Jacob Hester subsequently handled the transition to a commercial break. The clip circulated on social media, drawing attention to the unusual exchange during an otherwise routine halftime interview. LSU Coach Issues Public Apology Kiffin opened his Monday news conference by addressing the incident. “I want to apologize for my language at halftime in the interview,” Kiffin said. “No excuses.” He acknowledged his frustration with the first half and said he had difficulty hearing the question because of the noise inside Neyland Stadium. However, the coach made clear that neither circumstance justified his language. “But there’s no reason for that,” Kiffin said. “And so, to people who were offended, I apologize for that.” Although Kiffin apologized for his wording, he maintained his disagreement with the targeting penalty. Benefield was ejected following a tackle on Tennessee tight end DaSaahn Brame late in the second quarter. The penalty helped extend Tennessee’s possession, which ended with Brame catching the go-ahead touchdown. Kiffin subsequently questioned the application of the targeting rule while discussing the play with reporters. Frustrations Mount During Difficult LSU Season The controversy comes during a disappointing stretch for LSU in Kiffin’s first season leading the program. The Tigers have lost three consecutive games, falling to Alabama, Texas and Tennessee during November. LSU enters its regular-season finale against Arkansas with a 6-5 record, including a 3-5 mark in Southeastern Conference play. Kiffin has repeatedly emphasized his confidence in the program’s future while acknowledging the team’s difficulty finishing close games. During his Sunday conference call, the coach also indicated that LSU would evaluate multiple aspects of the program after the season. “We’ll look at everything,” Kiffin said, referencing positions, schemes and coaches. For now, LSU’s attention turns toward Saturday’s matchup with Arkansas in Fayetteville. However, Kiffin’s latest viral moment has provided another reminder of the scrutiny surrounding his turbulent debut season in Baton Rouge. title: Leonard Moore a finalist for award for impact on and off the field
summary: Leonard Moore is known for his impact on the field, but his positive presence off it is why he's a finalist for a top defensive player award.
content: Junior defensive back Leonard Moore is considered a solid defender not just for Notre Dame, but in college football as a whole . His presence is felt on the field, but what he has done off it is worth noting. On Wednesday, Moore was named a finalist for the Lott IMPACT Trophy, which is awarded to the nation’s top defensive player “who also makes an impact off the field,” according to a description . A Unanimous All-American last season, Moore has provided 20 tackles, a forced fumble and seven pass deflections for the US LBM Coaches Poll No. 3 Fighting Irish so far this season. According to Notre Dame Athletics Moore, off the field, leads initiatives “to combat chronic absenteeism and inspire student success through mentorship and accountability” through Tackle Attendance South Bend. Moore founded the community-driven initiative and focused on “creating a culture of accountability and encouragement, the program unites schools, families, and local partners to provide mentorship, resources, and innovative engagement tools,” noted in the description. “Tackle Attendance is dedicated to helping students stay engaged, build positive habits and reach their full potential,” the description continued. The winner of the Lott IMPACT Trophy will be decided through a national voter poll. The award winner will be presented in Newport Beach (CA) on Dec. 9 at The Pacific Club. The most impactful defensive player in the country. title: LSU assistant coach named Broyles Award finalist
summary: LSU football defensive coordinator Blake Baker was nominated for an award given to the nation's top assistant coach.
content: LSU football nominated defensive coordinator Blake Baker for the Broyles Award, which is given annually to the top college football assistant coach in country. Last season, Baker was a semifinalist for the recognition. Over his tenure in Baton Rouge, the LSU defense progressed with its play on the field as well as recruiting high school prospects and transfer portal players. LSU ranks fourth in the country and first in the SEC in total defense. It has the second most sacks in the country with 42, trailing only Tennessee. The purple and gold have the most sack yards with 265 and rank fourth in first-down defense. Blake Baker is our nominee for the Broyles Award, recognizing the top assistant coach in the country pic.twitter.com/ivP8EESs5P — LSU Football (@LSUfootball) November 24, 2026 Baker is one of 12 SEC assistants on the list . Here are the SEC nominees: Alabama: Kane Wommack, defensive coordinator Florida: Evan McKissack, tight ends coach Georgia: Mike Bobo, offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach Kentucky: Cutter Leftwich, offensive line coach LSU: Blake Baker, defensive coordinator Oklahoma: Miguel Chavis, defensive ends coach Ole Miss : John Garrison, running game coordinator/offensive line coach South Carolina: Kendal Briles, offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach Tennessee: Jim Knowles, defensive coordinator Texas: Will Muschamp, defensive coordinator Texas A&M: Patrick Dougherty, special teams coordinator Vanderbilt: Melvin Rice, safeties coach Baker's defense has been tough to move the ball against when it matters most. LSU is holding opponents to a 30.8% conversion rate on third down, tied for ninth in the country and third in the SEC. Opposing quarterbacks have also struggled to find the end zone, as the Tigers have allowed just nine passing touchdowns, tied for seventh nationally and second in the SEC behind Tennessee. title: Mizzou Faces Old School Test Saturday Against Old Rival
summary: The Tigers have faced their fair share of slugfests against Oklahoma. Saturday might be the latest physical battle.
content: For 89 years, Missouri belonged to a conference defined by a ground and pound style of football where corn-fed physicality reigned supreme. The Big Eight was one of the most geographically and culturally tight-knit conferences in the sport. It was the product of an era where the similarities shared by a group of universities and its fanbases — not how much money they could collectively get in a media rights deal — determined who you played each season. MU gets to relive some of that history Saturday when it hosts old foe Oklahoma, one of the new(er) kids on the block in the SEC and the Tigers’ designated rival at the end of the regular season. For their part, the Sooners are already rekindling some of that Big Eight magic with a late season hot streak spurred by a resurgent run game. Oklahoma’s offense was barely animate for much of the season, a big reason why the squad limped to a 4-4 start despite having an elite defensive unit. But after a resounding loss to South Carolina, head coach Brent Venables finally pulled the plug and replaced offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle with Jason Witten. Three straight wins — including a pair of victories over ranked opponents in Ole Miss and Florida — followed the switch. “They’ve found their identity with coach Witten and their offensive coordinator adjustment,” Drinkwitz said, “He’s really doing a good job; they established the run.” The Sooners are averaging roughly five more points per game under Witten. As Drinkwitz alluded to, much of that improvement can be credited to their ground game. OU averaged just under 105 yards per game and an average of merely 3.09 yards per carry during conference play during its 2-3 start to conference play. Those numbers have jumped to more than 161 yards per game and 3.84 yards per carry under Witten. And much of that improvement can be seen directly in the Sooners’ signal caller. “John Mateer has been an excellent quarterback,” Drinkwitz said, “[He] has played his best ball these last three games.” The former Washington State transfer was mostly a non-factor in the running game for most of the season, collecting about 15 yards per game and 1.3 yards per carry against SEC opponents. But the switch to Witten as the offensive coordinator completely transformed Mateer, who has collected more than 50 yards on the ground in each of his past three games and averaged a far more robust 3.84 yards per carry during that stretch. Mizzou linebacker Nicholas Rodriguez had a simple answer for how to stop Oklahoma’s suddenly potent rushing attack: “Have to have gap integrity and just be physical.” That might be easier said than done, especially for a Tigers squad that has struggled with run defense each of the past two weeks against Georgia and Kentucky. Death Row Defense was one of the top units in the SEC at stopping the run across its first six games of conference play, allowing just under 105 yards per game with an average of just 3.25 yards per carry. Since then, Georgia ran for 182 yards on 5.4 yards per carry before the Wildcats averaged 4.5 yards per run and put up 158 yards on the ground overall. MU forced multiple turnovers and consistently clutched up against Kentucky in the red zone last week on the way to a 28-14 win. But the Tigers needed those red zone stops in the first place because UK was consistently able to gash them for chunk yardage on the ground and march down the field. Rodriguez was part of the uncharacteristic performance from Mizzou’s defense. He had multiple costly missed tackles against the Wildcats, a stark contrast to his normal stonewall performance against the run. The Tigers can’t afford a third straight down week from the strongest part of their defense as they face a team that’s found its groove on offense late in the season. This matchup will likely be defined by the same things as so many previous games between these two squads: who can dominate the trenches and stop the run. “It’s always a nice defensive game; I feel like it’s a hard-fought battle,” Rodriguez said, “We understand we may not like each other, but it’s a good time to just go out there and be physical and play for something — and this week we’re playing for the seniors.” Whether or not Mizzou’s seniors get to take a rock and be carried off the field in their final game at Faurot may be determined the old fashioned way — a physical slugfest. For a lot of Tigers fans who remember the countless times MU and the Sooners squared off as Big Eight opponents, I’d imagine they wouldn’t have it any other way.

title: No. 16 Arizona's Noah Fifita heads into home finale with his legacy secured
summary: (AP) — Noah Fifita has the arm to fit balls into incredibly tight spaces, mobility to turn negative plays into positive ones, intelligence to understand nearly every situation on a football field.He's ultracompetitive, a proven winner, his name prominent throughout Arizona's record book.
content: TUCSON, Ariz. (AP) — Noah Fifita has the arm to fit balls into incredibly tight spaces, mobility to turn negative plays into positive ones, intelligence to understand nearly every situation on a football field. He's ultracompetitive, a proven winner, his name prominent throughout Arizona's record book. He's a leader on and off the field, with his voice and his actions. He's unflinchingly loyal, generous, intertwined with the Tucson community. In other words, Noah Fifita is everything you'd would want in a quarterback — and a person. “I don't know if I'll be around another like him,” Arizona offensive coordinator Seth Doege said. “He's the greatest human being I've ever been around.” Fifita will pen the penultimate chapter of his college career Saturday against Arizona State in the 100th playing of the Territorial Cup rivalry. He and the 16th-ranked Wildcats (No. 16 CFP) still have a yet-to-be-determined bowl game to play, but his home finale will be the big send-off in one of the greatest careers in Arizona football history. Fifita arrived in Tucson as an undersized three-star quarterback out of Servite High School in Anaheim, California. He has had an oversized impact at Arizona since taking over as starter for the injured Jayden de Laura in 2023. The 5-foot-10 quarterback played so well he kept the starting job when de Laura returned, throwing for 2,869 yards and 25 touchdowns with six interceptions while setting a school record by completing 72.4% of his passes. The records kept coming. Fifita set the school single-season record with 2,958 yards passing in 2024 and broke the school record for TD passes in a season with 29 in 2025. He was the Big 12 first-team quarterback last season, the first at Arizona since 1975, and the second quarterback in program history to lead the team to two nine-win seasons. Fifita set the Arizona career record for touchdown passes (99) last season and became Arizona's all-time passing leader this season, at 12,656 yards and counting. He is second nationally this season with 3,473 yards passing, fourth in completion percentage at 71.4% and is tied for fifth with 26 TD passes. “In terms of how he’s viewed going forward, I think he’s viewed as the best quarterback to ever play at the University of Arizona,” Arizona head coach Brent Brennan said. “I think about what he has meant to this university. He also might be the best human being to ever play football at the University of Arizona.” The human part sets Fifita apart. In a transfer portal era of players hopscotching from team to team, Fifita opted to remain loyal. He started at Arizona and vowed to finish there, opening the season as one of five senior quarterbacks in the Bowl Subdivision to play their entire careers at the same school. Fifita potentially cost himself millions of NIL dollars by staying in Tucson but wanted to be there for his teammates until the end, solidifying his legacy while getting a chance to play with his brother Dash, a freshman linebacker, for the first time in their lives. “They’ve been loyal to me, they’ve trusted me, so I’ve been loyal to them,” Fifita said. “You want to prove them right and to the players in the locker room.” Fifita is as generous as he his loyal. When Arizona wins a game, Fifita does not talk to the media so his teammates can shine. When the Wildcats lose, Fifita is front and center answering questions, often taking the blame himself. Fifita also has stitched himself in the fabric of the Tucson community. He coaches flag football and runs a football camp. He hosts monthly community events and has barbeques at his house for teammates, often with Hawaiian specialties. Fifita showed up at the birthday party for Doege's daughter unannounced, presents in hand. He did something similar for defensive coordinator Danny Gonzales, appearing at a restaurant with balloons and flowers for his daughter's birthday. Fifita's contributions on and off the field made him a finalist for the Wuerffel Trophy, awarded to the FBS player who best combines exemplary community service with athletic and academic achievement. “When you have a kid I think who has the foresight like Noah to say, ‘Man, I could be remembered here forever; like, they may build a statue of me one day; like, I will be remembered,’” Arizona State coach Kenny Dillingham said. “I think he’s just a special human to be able to process, one, wanting to stay loyal to something in this era.” The Fifita era in Arizona is about to end. It will have a lasting impact on everyone he touched along the way. ___ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here , visit the Top 25 here and see AP’s full college football coverage here

title: Queens Park Rangers vs Sheffield United – Preview
summary: Sheffield United travel down to the capital on Saturday afternoon to face Queens Park Rangers in the EFL Championship.Queens Park Rangers enter this fixture in decent form having gone unbeaten in thei...
content: Queens Park Rangers vs Sheffield United – Preview Sheffield United travel down to the capital on Saturday afternoon to face Queens Park Rangers in the EFL Championship. Queens Park Rangers enter this fixture in decent form having gone unbeaten in their last four games; two draws and two wins, with their most recent result being a 1-1 draw against Norwich City. The Blades were involved in an exciting 1-1 draw against Southampton on Tuesday evening in what was a tale of two halves. United were dominated for the first 30 minutes but gradually grew into the contest before completely controlling the proceedings in the second period and earning a point. Team News The home side will be without defender Amadou Salif Mbengue after the Senegalese man suffered a season-ending cruciate ligament injury in October. Chris Wilder welcomed Kalvin Phillips back to the bench in midweek and was subsequently brought on in the second half. Patrick Bamford again started as a substitute, and was introduced at half-time to replace Tom Cannon. Perhaps both men will be in the starting eleven at the weekend. Queens Park Rangers’ Impact Player For This Game Queens Park Rangers will be looking towards Richard Kone to provide the attacking threat when they welcome Sheffield United to Loftus Road on Saturday afternoon. The striker has been one of Rangers’ most important attacking outlets this season, with his ability to combine physicality, movement and a willingness to shoot making him a difficult opponent for Championship defences. He has already registered five league goals and an assist, making him QPR’s leading goal contributor heading into the fixture. Kone is averaging 2.8 shots per 90, with 1.4 efforts on target, showing his willingness to test opposition goalkeepers. He is also producing 0.55 expected goals per 90, ranking among the Championship’s more dangerous forwards for chance generation. What makes the Ivorian particularly dangerous is his ability to operate as more than a traditional striker. His movement across the frontline, willingness to run in behind and ability to attack crosses give QPR different ways of threatening United’s defensive line. Sheffield United’s Impact Player For This Game SHEFFIELD, ENGLAND – NOVEMBER 21: Jordan Ayew (R) of Sheffield United celebrates scoring the third goal during the Sky Bet Championship 2026/27 match between Sheffield United and Watford at Bramall Lane on November 21, 2026 in Sheffield, England. (Photo by Nigel Roddis/Getty Images) Jordan Ayew looks an excellent candidate to make the difference when Sheffield United travel to Queens Park Rangers on Saturday, particularly after producing two impressive performances at Bramall Lane against Watford and Southampton. The Ghanaian international was one of United’s standout performers against Southampton on Tuesday evening, earning an 8.05 FotMob rating despite the Blades being held to a 1-1 draw. Ayew registered an assist for Sydie Peck’s dramatic 90th-minute equaliser, alongside two shots, one on target and two key passes. He also played a crucial role in United’s 4-0 victory over Watford, scoring the third goal. His underlying numbers further show his growing influence as a Sheffield United player. Ayew is averaging 0.4 goals, 0.2 assists, 1.6 successful dribbles and 8.4 duels won per 90 in the Championship this season. He also averages two tackles per 90 and 3.4 defensive contributions per 90, highlighting his willingness to press, track and contribute defensively. Throughout his career, Ayew has always been recognised for his versatility, and Blades fans are now seeing this in a red and white shirt. He can operate centrally or drift into wider areas, using his close control, strength and experience to bring others into play and draw fouls. Look for the Ghanaian to be influential for the Blades once more. My Prediction Queens Park Rangers currently reside in seventh, while the Blades sit in ninth-place. This should be an entertaining game, with both clubs riding some good momentum and form. Sheffield United have had a great time of things in recent times at Loftus Road; they’ve won on four of their last five visits, including one draw. And after their excellent second half performance against the Saints, I expect the Blades to build on that performance and secure a 3-1 victory in this one. Stats taken from Fotmob.

title: Recruiting Roundup: 2 newest commits explains why they chose Michigan Football
summary: River Rouge’s Jerrimiah Cross wants to play both ways in Ann Arbor. Landon Hall went from a playoff comeback to a Michigan commitment in five days, and Cass Tech’s Mylan Griggs explains why home still matters after a fall on the road.
content: Welcome to the Recruiting Roundup, our twice-per-week series breaking down the latest developments on the recruiting trail for the Michigan Wolverines. We’ll keep you up to date on the top targets, the visits they take, the predictions that analysts make, and everything in between. Here’s what you need to know today… Michigan’s two-way plans sold Jerrimiah Cross 2028 three-star athlete Jerrimiah Cross grew up rooting for Michigan. When it came time to pick a school, the Wolverines gave the River Rouge junior another reason to stay home. They were one of the few programs willing to give him a shot at both wide receiver and cornerback. Cross chose Michigan over Michigan State, Arizona State and Virginia Tech on Tuesday, becoming the Wolverines’ first commitment in the 2028 class. The Rivals Industry Rankings list him as the No. 119 receiver nationally and the No. 23 prospect in Michigan. “I’m comfortable playing wherever the team needs me, but I know they like me at both receiver and corner,” Cross told The Michigan Insider’s Brice Marich . Cross gave Michigan plenty of film to work with at both spots this fall. He caught 51 passes for 910 yards and 12 touchdowns. At corner, he made 32 tackles, broke up seven passes, forced two fumbles and picked off two passes. Landon Hall goes from a playoff comeback to a Michigan commitment Last Friday, Landon Hall had two minutes to erase an 11-point deficit and keep Mishawaka (Ind.) Penn’s undefeated season alive. He pulled it off, leading Penn to a 49-45 win and a spot in the state title game. The next day, his brothers watched as Kyle Whittingham offered him a scholarship on his first visit to Michigan. “Their main reason was that I was a winner,” Hall told The Wolverine’s Ethan McDowell . Hall initially planned to get through Friday’s state championship game before turning his attention back to recruiting. By Wednesday, he’d made up his mind. The three-star quarterback committed to Michigan, joining Kamden Lopati as the second passer in the Wolverines’ 2027 class. “Getting to experience The Big House and the fans there, it was a pretty crazy environment to be in,” Hall said. “It was definitely the craziest atmosphere I’ve ever been in.” Through 13 games, Hall has completed 77.6 percent of his passes for 3,253 yards. He threw 51 touchdown passes against just three interceptions and ran for four more scores. Now he gets to play for a state title with his college decision already made. Cass Tech’s Mylan Griggs explains why Michigan is still in the mix Detroit Cass Tech’s Mylan Griggs used the fall to see schools farther from home, including UCLA and Washington. The 2028 four-star wide receiver already knew Ann Arbor well after several visits over the past two years, and he still made it back for the UTEP game. Asked what keeps him interested in Michigan, Griggs brought it back to Detroit. “I’m a city kid, man,” Griggs told The Wolverine’s McDowell . “I love home. I just love home. I believe in them. I think they can change it around.” Griggs topped 1,000 all-purpose yards, scored nine touchdowns and intercepted four passes as Cass Tech reached the state semifinals. Michigan is recruiting him at receiver, where the Rivals Industry Rankings have him No. 39 nationally at that position. He’s the No. 6 prospect in the state. He plans to narrow his list now that his junior season is over. Michigan and Michigan State are both in the mix alongside Nebraska, UCLA, Washington and Missouri. Position coach Micah Simon has spent the past year getting to know Griggs, who also stays in regular contact with assistant director of player personnel Richard Perry.

title: Schumacher 'can't flog' in-form striker Dalby
summary: Bolton boss Steven Schumacher says he will manage Sam Dalby's workload after he started the 3-1defeat by West Brom on the bench.
content: Bolton will have to manage in-form striker Sam Dalby's workload after he started on the bench in Wednesday's 3-1 home defeat by West Bromwich Albion, boss Steven Schumacher has said. The 26-year-old had scored three goals in the four Championship games leading up to the Albion match but was replaced in the starting line-up by Theo Bair, only to come on for the Canada international at half-time with the scoreline 1-0 to the visitors. Dalby has started 14 of Bolton's first 17 Championship matches so far as the club await Ryan Hardie's return to full fitness. Chris Forino-Joseph was also introduced at the interval in a double change by Schumacher as Bolton found an equaliser after the hour-mark but were unable to keep hold of a point. "Obviously, I know how good a player he [Dalby] is but I can't flog him and make him play 46 games, 90 minutes every week," Schumacher told BBC Radio Manchester. "It's just not possible. Plus, I've got another striker who is desperate for an opportunity. "I thought it was the right call to try and freshen up the team but it was a difficult night for us in the first half and Theo did have a big chance and headed it over. "But yes, I thought the changes were necessary at half-time." All the latest Bolton Wanderers news

title: Throwback Thursday: When Zero Seconds Were Just Enough for Notre Dame vs Syracuse
summary: A missed field goal, a controversial penalty, and a second chance that changed college football's rules.
content: There have been plenty of memorable finishes throughout Notre Dame football history, but few have generated quite as much controversy as what transpired at Notre Dame Stadium on November 18, 1961. On that cold November afternoon, the Fighting Irish defeated Syracuse 17–15 on a field goal kicked after time had expired. What followed was a national debate involving football officials, conference commissioners, university presidents, and the NCAA itself. And if that weren’t enough, the game would ultimately help bring about a change to the college football rule book. For this week’s Throwback Thursday, we’re traveling back 65 years to revisit a game that was over according to the scoreboard but was far from over in just about every other respect. The Orangemen Come to South Bend Syracuse arrived in South Bend ranked No. 10 in the country and just two years removed from its 1959 national championship. Under head coach Ben Schwartzwalder, the Orangemen had established themselves as one of the nation’s premier football programs, led by the extraordinarily talented Ernie Davis, who would soon become the first African American to win the Heisman Trophy. Notre Dame, meanwhile, was in its third season under head coach Joe Kuharich. The Irish entered the game with a 4–3 record, having snapped a three-game losing streak the previous weekend against Pittsburgh. A victory over nationally ranked Syracuse would certainly provide a bright spot in what had been an inconsistent season. The matchup marked Syracuse’s first appearance at Notre Dame Stadium, and the excitement surrounding the game extended well beyond South Bend. According to historical Syracuse newspaper accounts referenced in a 2025 Sports Illustrated retrospective, approximately 5,000 Syracuse fans traveled to Indiana for the game, while more than 7,000 others purchased tickets to watch a closed-circuit broadcast at Syracuse’s downtown War Memorial. The game was not among those being televised by ABC that afternoon, so thousands of fans gathered to experience it together. For Syracuse, there were postseason implications as well. The Orangemen had their sights set on an Orange Bowl invitation, giving their November visit to Notre Dame even greater significance. Little did anyone know that the most important play of the afternoon would occur after the clock had reached zero. A Tale of Two Halves Despite Syracuse’s national ranking and impressive credentials, it was Notre Dame that controlled much of the afternoon. The Irish jumped out to a 14–0 lead and maintained that advantage until late in the third quarter. With the Orangemen struggling to generate offense, Schwartzwalder decided it was time to take a chance. Facing fourth-and-one, Syracuse used the threat of Ernie Davis to its advantage. A fake handoff to Davis helped set up a long touchdown pass, and a successful two-point conversion cut Notre Dame’s lead to 14–8. Syracuse struck again on its next possession, scoring on a short touchdown pass and taking a 15–14 advantage in the fourth quarter. Suddenly, a game that Notre Dame had largely controlled was slipping away. Syracuse had the momentum, the lead, and an opportunity to escape South Bend with a victory. But the Orangemen were unable to put the game away, failing to convert a crucial fourth down and giving Notre Dame one final possession with just 17 seconds remaining. Seventeen seconds. Not much time to travel into field goal range, especially in an era when long-distance field goals were considerably less routine than they are today. But as Notre Dame fans have learned countless times throughout the years, sometimes a few seconds are all the Irish need. When Zero Seconds Were Just Enough Taking possession at Notre Dame’s own 20-yard line, Irish quarterback Frank Budka immediately went to work. According to a 2005 Notre Dame Athletics retrospective, Budka ran for 21 yards and then completed a 10-yard pass to George Sefcik, putting Notre Dame in position to attempt a desperation 56-yard field goal. With only a few seconds remaining, Joe Perkowski lined up for what appeared to be Notre Dame’s final opportunity. His kick was unsuccessful, and Syracuse players began celebrating what they believed was a hard-fought victory. Time had expired, and the Orangemen had apparently completed their comeback. But there was a penalty flag on the field. Syracuse’s Walt Sweeney had made contact with Perkowski, with the collision also involving holder George Sefcik. The officials assessed a 15-yard penalty against Syracuse and awarded Notre Dame another opportunity, despite the fact that there was no time remaining on the clock. Perkowski lined up again, this time from 41 yards. His second attempt sailed through the uprights, giving Notre Dame a stunning 17–15 victory and sending the Irish faithful into celebration. Perkowski became the first kicker in Notre Dame football history to win a game on its final play. For Notre Dame fans, it was an improbable finish worth celebrating. For Syracuse fans, it was a devastating reversal of fortune. And for college football officials, it was the beginning of a rather significant headache. When the Rule Book Entered the Conversation In the days following the game, the controversy quickly spread beyond South Bend and Syracuse. By November 21, United Press International was reporting that all five game officials had been ordered to submit written reports to Big Ten Commissioner William Reed and Eastern Intercollegiate Football Association Commissioner Asa Bushnell. At the heart of the controversy was an unusual provision in the NCAA football rule book. According to the contemporary newspaper coverage, the rules stipulated that when a team clearly intended to kick, “any foul during the kick, including roughing the kicker, will not extend the period as the ball is not in the kicking team’s possession.” Essentially, under that interpretation, Notre Dame had relinquished possession of the football when Perkowski attempted his original field goal. Because time had expired, the penalty against Syracuse should not have resulted in an additional play. Bushnell indicated that any decision regarding the officials’ actions would not change the outcome of the contest. Whether the result would stand was another matter entirely, and one that would ultimately rest with the universities themselves. Meanwhile, Syracuse’s postseason prospects remained a topic of discussion. Just three days after the game, The Oregon Statesman reported that the Orangemen had the inside track for an invitation to the December 16 Liberty Bowl, despite their controversial defeat. The newspaper rather modestly described the national debate over the winning field goal as a “fuss brewing.” As it turned out, that was something of an understatement. When Football Became a University Affair By November 24, newspapers were reporting that Notre Dame was considering severing athletic relations with Syracuse. The disagreement had reached the highest levels of university leadership, involving Notre Dame President Father Theodore Hesburgh and Syracuse Chancellor William P. Tolley. Notre Dame officials denied reports that the university intended to concede the victory and maintained that the Irish had won under the rules. Four days later, General Robert Neyland, athletic director at the University of Tennessee and chairman of the NCAA football rules committee, announced that Notre Dame had been officially advised that its winning field goal was illegal. However, as Neyland explained in an Associated Press report published on November 28, there was no mechanism for reversing the outcome. “There is no authority, no redress, once a game ends,” Neyland said. “The score cannot be changed unless Notre Dame wants to acknowledge that the game belongs to Syracuse.” Notre Dame was not prepared to do that, nor was the university prepared to accept Neyland’s interpretation without further discussion. A United Press International report published the following day indicated that Notre Dame officials had demanded a formal decision from the NCAA rules committee. An unnamed Notre Dame athletic official accused Neyland of compounding what he described as “a serious injustice to Notre Dame.” Eleven days after Perkowski’s winning field goal had sailed through the uprights, the Irish were still defending their victory. The Battle of the Rule Book What makes this controversy particularly fascinating is that Notre Dame’s argument wasn’t based simply on an unwillingness to surrender a victory. The university believed that another provision in the NCAA rule book supported the officials’ decision. On November 30, the Medford Mail Tribune reported that NCAA President Henry Hardt had supported Neyland’s interpretation and that a letter conveying that position had been mailed to Notre Dame. Athletic director Moose Krause indicated that the university would withhold further comment until the official correspondence had been received. Notre Dame contended that the interpretation overlooked another rule stating that possession of the football remained with the kicking team “if a roughing-the-kicker penalty is accepted.” Under that provision, the Irish argued that they had retained possession and that the officials were justified in allowing another play. It was an interesting dilemma. If the rules allowed a defending team to rough the kicker on the final play of a game without giving the kicking team another opportunity, what was to prevent a team from deliberately doing so? Notre Dame’s official 2005 retrospective describes an eventual NCAA interpretation favorable to the Irish, while contemporary newspaper coverage documents the NCAA leadership’s initial determination that the extra play was illegal. Whatever the ultimate interpretation of the competing provisions, the official result remained Notre Dame 17, Syracuse 15. In February 1962, the NCAA revised its rules to clarify the treatment of accepted defensive penalties at the end of a game and prevent a similar situation from occurring again. The two universities met again at Yankee Stadium on Thanksgiving Day in 1963, just six days after the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. Syracuse won that meeting 14–7, and the two programs would not face one another again until 2003. An Unexpected Career Assist As fascinating as the football controversy itself was, perhaps my favorite discovery while researching this week’s story had absolutely nothing to do with football. In the summer 2013 issue of Notre Dame Magazine, Paul K. Rooney shared a wonderful recollection of the game following the death of former Syracuse player Walt Sweeney. Rooney had attended the game and remembered it as a dark, cold afternoon that hadn’t been particularly interesting until those unforgettable final seconds. Little did he know that Sweeney’s involvement in the controversial penalty would have an unexpected impact on his own career. The following week, Rooney traveled to New York City to apply for a position with the Wall Street law firm Simpson, Thacher & Bartlett. Arriving during the lunch hour, he was eventually directed to the office of partner Ira Hawkins. But rather than discussing Rooney’s academic credentials or legal aspirations, Hawkins pushed his résumé aside and asked about the Notre Dame-Syracuse game. Hawkins had listened to the game on the radio and wanted a firsthand account of what had happened. Rooney described the controversial penalty and the circumstances surrounding Perkowski’s winning field goal. When Hawkins asked whether Notre Dame would forfeit the game, Rooney told him he very much doubted it. Before long, Hawkins asked Rooney whether he wanted to work for the firm. Following another remarkably brief interview and a subsequent conversation with his dean back at Notre Dame, Rooney accepted the offer. More than five decades later, Rooney remembered Sweeney with a certain fondness, writing, “Little did I know that Sweeney was to make my day.” Sweeney would go on to enjoy an impressive professional football career as an All-Pro guard with the San Diego Chargers, while Rooney had a rather unusual story to tell about how he landed his job on Wall Street. Of all the unintended consequences of that controversial November afternoon in South Bend, this might just be the most delightful. A Victory That Still Stands Sixty-five years later, the 1961 Notre Dame-Syracuse game remains one of those wonderfully unusual chapters in college football history. A missed field goal, a penalty flag, and a second opportunity generated weeks of national headlines, threatened athletic relations between two universities, exposed conflicting provisions in the NCAA rule book, and ultimately helped change the rules of the game. One of the things I love most about researching these old Notre Dame football stories is discovering just how much history can be hidden behind a seemingly ordinary score in the record books. Without knowing the story behind it, Notre Dame’s 17–15 victory over Syracuse might look like little more than another close game from an otherwise unremarkable season. Instead, it turned out to be a game with consequences that extended far beyond Notre Dame Stadium. And somewhere in the middle of all that controversy was a Notre Dame law student who walked into a job interview expecting to discuss his résumé and ended up talking football instead. If that isn’t a classic Notre Dame story, I don’t know what is. As we gather around our Thanksgiving tables this week, I’m particularly grateful for the generations of Notre Dame fans who have kept these stories alive. Their recollections, the old newspaper clippings, and the little pieces of history tucked away in university archives make it possible for us to continue sharing these remarkable moments decades later. Sometimes, the most memorable moments in Notre Dame football history happen in the final seconds. And sometimes, there aren’t any seconds left at all. Go Irish! Beat Syracuse! Sources: “Notre Dame Is Told Goal Was Not Legal,” Associated Press, The News-Review, November 28, 1961. “Notre Dame May Sever Relations With Orange,” United Press International, Raleigh Register, November 24, 1961. Paul K. Rooney, Class Notes, Notre Dame Magazine, Summer 2013. “Notre Dame and Syracuse Meet for the Fifth Time,” FightingIrish.com, November 17, 2005. The Oregon Statesman, November 21, 1961, page 9. “Notre Dame Demanding Settlement,” United Press International, Medford Mail Tribune, November 29, 1961. “Officials to Rule on Irish Field Goal; Penalty Suspect,” United Press International, Medford Mail Tribune, November 21, 1961. title: Tide starters listed on Availability Report for Iron Bowl vs. Auburn
summary: Alabama received some good news on Wednesday night's initial Availability Report, while Auburn has a very important player whose status is unknown.
content: The initial SEC Availability Report for Saturday's Iron Bowl between Alabama and Auburn has been released, and for the Crimson Tide in particular, it appears a number of key players are trending in the right direction. Released on Wednesday night, Alabama had 11 total players listed on the initial report, seven of which will miss the Iron Bowl. Each of those seven listed were expected going into Wednesday night, meaning there were no surprises in terms of players listed as "out." However, there were in fact some surprises when it came to the others listed, as Alabama has four players officially carrying a "probable" tag ahead of the Iron Bowl. Among those were starting inside linebackers Luke Metz and Caleb Woodson, as well as rotational defensive lineman Fatutoa Henry. The biggest surprise though is outside linebacker Desmond Umeozulu, who was also listed as probable, and as a result, appears to be nearing a potential return in Week 13. Umeozulu, a senior transfer from South Carolina, has missed a majority of the season due to injury, and has not played since the Florida State game. For Auburn, undoubtedly the biggest takeaway from Wednesday night's report was starting quarterback Byrum Brown, who is listed as "questionable." Should Brown potentially miss the Iron Bowl, then backup Tristan Ti'a would likely get the start. Following is a look at Wednesday night's initial Week 13 Availability Report for the Iron Bowl showdown between Alabama and Auburn. Alabama vs. Auburn initial Iron Bowl SEC Availability Report Alabama: Jireh Edwards , Defensive Back - Out Cayden Jones , Linebacker - Out Mhari Johnson , Defensive Line - Out Nick Sherman , Defensive Back - Out Josh Ford , Tight End - Out Casey Poe , Offensive Line - Out Jeremiah Beaman , Defensive Line - Out Luke Metz , Linebacker - Probable Caleb Woodson , Linebacker - Probable Desmond Umeozulu , Linebacker - Probable Fatutoa Henry , Defensive Line - Probable Auburn: Bryce Deas , Linebacker - Out Gavin Jenkins , Cornerback - Out De'marcus Riddick , Linebacker - Questionable Byrum Brown , Quarterback - Questionable Contact/Follow us @RollTideWire on X (formerly Twitter) and like our page on Facebook to follow ongoing coverage of Alabama news, notes and opinion . title: Top 5 college football games to watch in Week 13
summary: 5 college football games with major stakes this weekend.
content: The final week of the 2026 college football regular season is here and "Rivalry Week", as it is lovingly known, is sure to deliver on Thanksgiving weekend. After Week 12 gave us some thrilling and unexpected results, a major shakeup to the month of November has left us with a delicious Week 13 slate. Though some of the more well-known rivalries aren't as interesting this year as they have been in years past, it just means that some more under-the-radar rivalry games will get their moment in the sun this week. It's also the last full weekend of the season with every team still playing. Everyone who gets to play after this week of games has earned it. Here at Sooners Wire, we'll be all over the big game on the docket for the Oklahoma Sooners this weekend , and it's just one of many exciting matchups in a very interesting group of regular-season finales. Here are the top five games to watch in Week 13. 1. USC at UCLA, Saturday at 2:30 p.m. CT USC and UCLA haven't both been this good at the same time in a while, and they'll face off in Pasadena in a game that is extremely important to the Big Ten title game race. The Trojans are still technically alive in the standings to get to the conference championship game, but head coach Lincoln Riley's team would need a lot of help to get there. Instead, they're hoping for a convincing win and some chaos in front of them to allow them to sneak into the College Football Playoff as an at-large team. Quarterback Jayden Maiava and the offense will need to be on-point against a very strong defense. The Bruins saw their unbeaten season fall apart in last week's loss to Michigan, and new head coach Bob Chesney has had to navigate several quarterback injuries this season. Starter Nico Iamaleava went down weeks ago, with backup Ty Diffenbach filling in nicely in his stead. When Diffenbach was injured last week, Madden Iamaleava was forced into action, and the offense faltered. Diffenbach could potentially be in line to return this week, and this team can go to the Big Ten title game if they get a home win in the Rose Bowl on Saturday. 2. Oklahoma at Missouri, Saturday at 3:15 p.m. CT Oklahoma and Missouri play in the SEC's biggest game this week, as both programs have navigated treacherous schedules to land themselves in a good position heading into the final week of the regular season. The Sooners have won three straight games after a 4-4 start, and head coach Brent Venables has his team one win away from another undefeated November. Quarterback John Mateer has rebounded over the last three weeks, and he's playing confident football again. It's not in time to get OU to the CFP, but he's looking to finish strong on the road in Columbia. The Tigers are also out of the CFP race, but after beating Kentucky last week, they're also looking to finish the season on a high note. Head coach Eliah Drinkwitz can still put his team in a very good bowl game, and this squad can play like one of the SEC's best when they're on their game. Quarterback Austin Simmons has quietly put together one of the best seasons in the conference, and Mizzou will have a rowdy crowd in CoMo behind them. The home team has won this game for each of the last two seasons. 3. Nebraska at Iowa, Friday at 11:00 a.m. CT Nebraska and Iowa might play in one of the best environments in the country this weekend, as both teams are looking to keep winning streaks going to close out the regular season. The Cornhuskers are out of the Big Ten title race, but last week's big win over Ohio State has them believing they can pull off another upset this week. Head coach Matt Rhule needed that victory in a big win, and going on the road to Iowa City and winning on Rivalry Week would go a long way for the program. To do that, the 'Huskers will need quarterback Anthony Colandrea to play like a star against a strong defense. The Hawkeyes are in the CFP race and the Big Ten title race, with somewhat realistic paths to both, though not extremely likely at this point. However, head coach Kirk Ferentz's team is certainly not out of it, and four-straight wins have elevated them into the conversation. Quarterback Hank Brown has regained the starting job from Jeremy Hecklinski, and he'll look to play mistake-free football and lead the offense to success. Kinnick Stadium should be rocking on Friday afternoon, and the Hawkeyes will look to make it four-straight wins in the Heroes Game. 4. Washington at Oregon, Saturday at 6:30 p.m. CT Washington and Oregon will renew their rivalry this week in another game crucial to the Big Ten title race during Rivalry Week. The Huskies are not able to make the conference championship game, but they can ruin their hated rival's chances, which is really what this week is all about. Head coach Jedd Fisch has seen his team rebound after a tough stretch, and last week's upset win over Indiana opened the door for another big showcase this week. Quarterback Demond Williams Jr. will need to take care of the football against a talented defense, but he's got star power, as he showed last week. The Ducks have a very good shot to make the Big Ten title game, and that could catapult them back into the playoff for the third straight year. Head coach Dan Lanning's team has rebounded from a rough patch earlier this season to fight back into the national conversation after it looked like they were done for. With star quarterback Dante Moore out for the season, backup Dylan Raiola has settled in and operated the offense very well over the last four weeks. Eugene should be rocking with a big rival coming to town and an unexpected opportunity on the table on Saturday night. 5. Louisville at Kentucky, Saturday at 11:00 a.m. CT Louisville and Kentucky have both fallen out of their respective conference races and the CFP race, but they are still two really good football teams with plenty of bragging rights on the line Saturday afternoon in Lexington for the Governor's Cup. The Cardinals have won six straight games, and head coach Jeff Brohm has one of the hottest teams in the country heading into Rivalry Week. Quarterback Lincoln Kienholz was a terrific find in the transfer portal, and the 'Cards are looking for a strong finish to another good year. The Wildcats started off very well, but they've fallen apart in recent weeks, losing three straight games. New head coach Will Stein in building something strong, but his team didn't peak at the right time in his first season. Still, the 'Cats were demolished in this game last year, so they have revenge on their minds on Saturday. Quarterback Kenny Minchey and the offense will need to keep pace in a game that could very well turn into a shootout. title: UNC football vs. NC State Wolfpack game info, streaming, betting
summary: UNC hosts NC State Saturday with bowl eligibility on the line for both ACC rivals. Here's our game preview with everything you need to know.
content: For two, in-state ACC football opponents who absolutely hate each other, they face off Saturday afternoon for more than just any old rivalry game. On November 28 at 12 p.m., UNC will host NC State with bowl eligibility on the line . North Carolina (5-6, 2-5 ACC) last beat the Wolfpack in the COVID-altered 2020 season, so there's immense pressure to snap the long skid on Thanksgiving weekend. With their 17-point win at UConn on November 7, the Tar Heels found themselves one win away from clinching their first postseason trip in two seasons. UNC returned home to host Louisville the following weekend, losing 16-14 despite holding the third-place Cardinals (8-3, 7-2 ACC) to 302, then suffered their worst defeat of 2026 in last weekend's 41-24 dud at Virginia. All of a sudden, the promise that once weaved its way into Chapel Hill is now gone. Head coach Bill Belichick is in danger of missing his second-straight postseason, which could be enough to make a coaching change. The Wolfpack (5-6, 3-5 ACC) had ACC title contention hopes, which Virginia quickly squashed in Week Zero. Star quarterback CJ Bailey is playing good football, but not living up to the star-level expectations media gave him. State has bad losses against Stanford, Duke and Syracuse, but won 28-10 at Florida State last weekend. Remember Bailey's infamous words upon Belichick's hiring ? North Carolina has a great chance to make Bailey eat his words on Saturday afternoon, ending the Pack's season and knocking them out of bowl contention. Can the Tar Heels end their season with a hard-to-come-by victory? Keep reading below for our game preview, which includes UNC's key to victory, something to watch, odds, statistical leaders and a season schedule. Key to Victory Limiting the big plays. When watching last weekend's game, how many times did you look at the screen and see a Virginia player running wide open? If you lost count, we don't blame you. North Carolina was slow to the ball-carrier and poor in pass coverage, allowing 461 yards and a season-worst 41 points. NC State scored 59 points and totaled 877 yards across its past two games. If the Tar Heels find a way to neutralize the Pack's explosiveness, they'll have an easier time winning a tough game. Something to Watch Who gets the start at quarterback. Billy Edwards took first-team reps on game day against Virginia, but true freshman Travis Burgess got the start. Burgess exceeded expectations and showcased himself as UNC's future, totaling 460 scrimmage yards and two touchdown, continuously making big plays with his arms and legs. North Carolina's season isn't over yet and, given his effectiveness in recent weeks, Edwards should get the start. Burgess is significantly more explosive, though, which could be exactly what the Tar Heels need for their greatest win since Drake Maye wore Carolina Blue. content: Mandatory Credit: Kiyoshi Mio-Imagn Images USC Trojans Marching Band banned from on-field performances vs. UCLA after ‘lewd’ vandalism appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The USC football team will face off against fierce rivals UCLA, whose Collge Football Playoff hopes hang in the balance. Trojans coach Lincoln Riley is all hyped up for the Battle of LA , but the Trojan Marching Band was a bit too hyped up and took the rivalry too far. Members of the Trojan Marching Band vandalized a part of the Bruins’ campus, removing letters from a sign outside of UCLA’s Wasserman Football Center to spell out a “lewd” phrase with them. That has led to the school banning the band from performing during pregame and halftime of the big game. “We want to express our deepest apologies to the entire UCLA community,” USC president Beong-Soo Kim said in the letter, per ESPN. “Our rivalry is one of the great traditions in college athletics, and it has always rested on mutual respect. What happened on UCLA’s campus last night has no place in this tradition.” Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Kim said any student found responsible will be disciplined under university policy and that the school is fully cooperating with the ongoing police investigation. No. 9 UCLA lost its undefeated record after suffering an 18-16 triple-overtime defeat to Michigan . The Bruins still lead the Big Ten at 7-1, though, and they would clinch a trip to the conference championship game by beating USC. Meanwhile, No. 15 USC is 5-3 and can also make it to the title game. However, the Trojans need to beat the Bruins and hope other results go their way. There are four teams (Indiana, Iowa, Oregon, and Wisconsin) currently above them in the standings. title: How to watch Nebraska football vs. Iowa: Time, TV channel
summary: It's Nebraska vs. Iowa in the regular-season football finale. Here's how to watch, including time, channel, TV schedule and streaming info.
content: The Nebraska Cornhuskers (7-4, 4-4) close out the 2026 regular season with the annual Black Friday matchup against the Iowa Hawkeyes (9-2, 6-2) at Kinnick Stadium. Nebraska is coming off a 31-28 victory over the No. 14 Ohio State Buckeyes last Saturday in Lincoln. The win was the Huskers' first over a ranked opponent since 2016 (a 35-31 win against the No. 22 Oregon Ducks ). Iowa enters Friday's game following a 34-17 win at Illinois last weekend. The Hawkeyes are on a four-game winning streak and are still in the running for a spot in the Big Ten Championship Game. Nebraska ranked No. 25 in last week's College Football Playoff rankings. It was the Huskers' first appearance since November of 2016. The selection committee ranked Iowa No. 15 last week. Friday's game marks the 37th straight season the Huskers have played the day after Thanksgiving. Nebraska is 20-16 on Black Friday since 1990. The Huskers were 5-1 against the Oklahoma Sooners from 1990 to 1995, 11-4 against the Colorado Buffaloes from 1996 to 2010, and are 4-11 against Iowa since 2011. Friday's game is the 57th all-time meeting between these two schools and the 16th meeting as Big Ten Conference opponents. Nebraska leads the series 30-23-3 all-time but Iowa has an 11-4 series lead as Big Ten opponents.
