title: Tiger Woods is making another comeback. Can his battered body hold up this time? | Opinion
summary: Tiger Woods is set to return at the Hero World Challenge. Despite injuries and criticism, he refuses to retire.
content: How the other half lives, huh? I was reading one of those “day in the life” articles over the weekend, and it featured some guy called Scotch McClure, who is a big shot in the multibillion-dollar world of longevity tech, although his name does sound like something you’d find on the drink specials at my local bar. Anyway, ahead of another busy day at work, Scotch gets up at the crack of dawn every morning to meditate. “It’s how I align my chakras and bring my body and mind into coherence,” declared Scotch. I’m not sure what, or where, my own chakras are. My wife suggested they might be in that junk drawer with the Allen wrenches and obsolete phone chargers. But if I do stumble upon them, I can guarantee the damn things won’t be aligned. In fact, forget about aligning my chakras. I have enough trouble with the alignment in the setup of my golf swing, as the whole process, and inevitably disastrous results, drags my body and mind into complete incoherence. On the subject of the swing, I saw another article about research conducted by university psychologists that found golfers who think too much about technique can actually hurt their game. If it’s any help to the researchers, I’d like to add that the process of swinging a club at a ball is considerably easier when you don’t have any technique worth thinking about in the first place. I should be a psychologist, huh? More: What can we expect from Tiger Woods at the Hero? A review of his returns after long layoffs Next week, meanwhile, we’ll all get to see Tiger Woods swinging a club again for the first time in ages. You probably heard the news the other day that Tiger is set to make comeback No. 146, or something like that, in the 20-man, no-cut Hero World Challenge in the Bahamas. Now, I know Woods used to dabble in a bit of meditation, but since his last competitive appearance in the 2024 Open at Royal Troon, there have been a few hits to the coherence of both body and mind. Those chakras have been all over the place. Three more surgeries, two on his back and one on his Achilles, added to the wear and tear on a body that creaks like an abandoned ship, while yet another car accident, a subsequent DUI charge and a stint in an inpatient rehab facility in Switzerland provided more dispiriting twists to the turbulent Tiger tale. But after all the trials and tribulations, it looks like he’ll be back. Again. Will it be another short-lived exercise in futility? Who knows, but rightly or wrongly, a good chunk of the golf world will no doubt be captivated by this latest, tentative return to competition. Nobody cranks up the “will he, won’t he” drama quite like Tiger. I realize, of course, that many of you reading this probably couldn’t care less about another Woods comeback. In fact, you may have stopped reading this column already. Can you keep going, please? There are only 500 or so words left. But I can understand the weary indifference toward a golfer and a man whose various off-course exploits in recent years have also stirred feelings of anger, sympathy, sadness, disappointment, morbid curiosity and bewilderment. And let’s face it, those of us who cover this game for a living probably don’t help matters. We continually push the Woods fantasies and go on about how he could still do this, maybe do a little of that and possibly accomplish something else despite his slide into competitive irrelevance. His various reappearances tend to get shoved down your throat with such overwhelming, unhinged force that it must feel like the entire golf media industry is stampeding right over you. We’ve said it many times before, and we’ll say it again. Woods has been golf’s blessing and its curse. He brings attention like nothing else but also overshadows everything else, even at 50, with his powers painfully diminished and the invincibility of his prime replaced by fragility, vulnerability, uncertainty, calamity and stupidity. Retirement, of course, is a word that has been bandied about plenty when it comes to Woods, but who are we to tell a 15-time major winner when to call it a career? Colin Montgomerie suggested several times in various publications that Woods should’ve said goodbye after his emotional, cap-waving walk over the Swilcan Bridge when he missed the cut in the 2022 Open at St. Andrews. When Woods got wind of that claim ahead of the 2024 Open at Troon, he delivered a cutting response. “Well, as a past champion, I’m exempt until I’m 60, Colin’s not,” Woods said. “He’s not a past champion. So, he doesn’t get the opportunity to make that decision. I do.” Ouch. Next year’s Open is at his beloved St. Andrews, while the U.S. Open returns to another of Tiger’s happy hunting grounds, Pebble Beach. Throw in the Masters at Augusta and one imagines he’ll be triply determined to be at all three, even if it amounts to a farewell tour. Many a great sports story involves an athlete crossing the finish line, but sometimes it’s no less compelling to see one simply get to the starting line. We’ve been on this journey many times with Woods. If all goes well, the road to recovery will continue next week. And on that note, I’m off to align my chakras. If I can find the damn things. Nick Rodger is the golf correspondent for the Scotland Herald, part of USA Today Co. This article originally appeared on Golfweek: Tiger Woods is making another comeback. Can his battered body hold up this time? | Opinion

title: "Tumor on My Brain and Liver": Pro Opens Up About Health Battle Weeks After Securing DP World Tour Card
summary: MJ Daffue had finally found his way back to the DP World Tour after a difficult couple of seasons. His fifth-place finish in the 2026 HotelPlanner Tour rankings earned his card for next year.
content: 190716 A golfer in silhouette during a practice round prior to the The 148th Open Golf Championship on July 16, 2019 in Portrush Photo Petter Arvidson BILDBYRAN kod PA 92322 BBeng golf the open the 148th Open British Open Royal Portrush The 148th Open Championship genre siluett, PUBLICATIONxNOTxINxDENxNORxSWExFINxAUT Copyright: PETTERxARVIDSON BB190716PA006 ©imago images / Bildbyran MJ Daffue had finally found his way back to the DP World Tour after a difficult couple of seasons. His fifth-place finish in the 2026 HotelPlanner Tour rankings earned his card for next year. But just weeks after celebrating that achievement, the South African has received news that has put his golfing plans on hold. The 37-year-old opened up about his health in an Instagram post on Thursday, revealing that doctors had discovered tumors on his brain and liver following a hospital stay. “Unfortunately, I ended up in the hospital with an infection about 10 days ago, and after lots of tests they could not find the source. However, they did find a Tumor on my brain and my liver. Many more tests later it was established that the one on my liver is benign, so we are very grateful. Unfortunately, the one on my brain is still a mystery. I am currently on strong medication to see if we can attack the [lesion] on the brain, but I am struggling a bit physically. I am in great spirits, and the care team and neurosurgeon have a perfect plan. I feel very confident that this is something that I will also kick butt and be ready to go soon,” Daffue wrote . While the liver tumor has been confirmed as benign, Daffue has not shared further details about the lesion on his brain, such as a definitive diagnosis or a timeline for his recovery. For now, his focus remains on treatment. Sky Sports reports that he will miss the start of the 2027 DP World Tour season. A golfer's resilience takes on new meaning when facing life's toughest challenges. Subscribe to stay updated on the inspiring stories reshaping professional golf. The timing is particularly difficult given the progress he made this year. Daffue started 2026 without a strong ranking on either the HotelPlanner Tour or the DP World Tour. That left him taking whatever playing opportunities came his way, often spending weeks away from home without knowing what his schedule would look like. He made the most of those chances. Daffue won the NTT DATA Pro-Am in February before claiming another victory at the DP World PGTI Open in India the following month. He also recorded three top-10 finishes on the DP World Tour before heading to Mallorca for the HotelPlanner Tour Grand Final. His third-place finish there lifted him to fifth in the final Road to Mallorca standings and secured his return to the DP World Tour for 2027. It was a significant turnaround for a player who had entered the season outside the world’s top 800. In a separate Instagram post celebrating his promotion, Daffue acknowledged how much the journey had demanded of him. He credited his wife for supporting him through the long stretches away from home and said he was proud that the sacrifices had paid off. He had been looking forward to carrying that momentum into the new season. Instead, the immediate priority has changed. Daffue thanked those who had reached out with messages of support and said he hoped to be back to full health and competing again soon. title: What Wyndham Clark found ‘shocking’ about the PGA Tour during his rookie year
summary: Wyndham Clark now has six PGA Tour titles to his name after a three-win season in 2026. Clark also added another major to his résumé after triumphing at the US Open at Shinnecock Hills this year.
content: Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images Wyndham Clark now has six PGA Tour titles to his name after a three-win season in 2026. Clark also added another major to his résumé after triumphing at the US Open at Shinnecock Hills this year. The 32-year-old has reestablished himself as one of the best players in the game this year, after going through real turmoil in 2025, both on and off the golf course. Wyndham Clark seems to be much happier in himself now, and that showed on the golf course throughout the 2026 PGA Tour season. Now that he has been around the block a few times, Clark has shared what some people do not realize about the PGA Tour when watching on their TV screens. What Wyndham Clark found ‘shocking’ about the PGA Tour during his rookie year The two-time major champion made an appearance on The Vanity Index Podcast and was asked what surprised him most about the PGA Tour when he first got his card. “ I would just say probably just the amount of golf you play, “ Clark replied. “ You play in college, you know, you play 11 or 12 events, and then you have your summer events, and it ends up being, you know, 16 to 18 events that you play. “ And then you get to the PGA Tour, and you’re playing 30 weeks because you’ve got to try and keep your card. Then because of how competitive it’s got, you can’t take time off like I was alluding to. “ You know, it’s just not as glamorous as people think. I think when you’re winning, and you’re in the limelight, and winning big tournaments, it’s amazing, but then there’s also just so much of a grind. “ The craziest thing is you play this big tournament, and then the next week, you’ve got another tournament, and it just is this never-ending cycle, and I just thought that was interesting. “ Everyone sees us on TV, like how glamorous it is, and, you know, you see the pretty stuff, but when you’re there on a Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and the travel Sunday night, and TSA and bags and all that stuff, it’s like, it’s a grind. I think that is, that was the most shocking. “ The good thing is that once you reach Wyndham Clark’s level, you don’t have to play 30 events anymore. For example, Clark played 25 tournaments on the PGA Tour throughout the 2026 season and that is around 5 more than the biggest names in the game usually play. It will be interesting to see whether he eases up on his schedule in 2027, with the 2028 PGA Tour season expected to be trimmed down to around 20 events.

title: 19 Hillsdale County volleyball athletes earn all-league SCAA-East
summary: Four Hillsdale County volleyball athletes earn highest honors from the SCAA conference. See the list of 2026 SCAA-East all-league athletes.
content: ILLSDALE COUNTY — Hillsdale County volleyball programs dominated the Southern Central Athletic Association East Division postseason honors following the 2026 fall sports season, accounting for all four Dream Team selections and 19 all-conference honorees. Hillsdale Academy seniors Lucy Cote and Malorie-Kate Apel and Pittsford juniors Alexis Bryner and Karmin Butler earned SCAA Dream Team honors, while Pittsford head coach Jessica Butler was named the division’s coach of the year. Butler led the Wildcats to a 21-12 overall record, their best finish since 2022, and an appearance in the Division 4 district championship game. Bryner, Cote and Apel also earned all-region honors from the Michigan Interscholastic Volleyball Coaches Association this fall. Hillsdale Academy earned six all-conference selections after finishing the season 23-9 and capturing its fourth consecutive district championship along with the division crown. Joining Cote and Apel with first-team honors was fellow senior Zoe Plemmons. Camden-Frontier junior Zailey Conroy rounded out Hillsdale County’s first-team selections. Local athletes accounted for six of the seven first-team honorees. Five more Hillsdale County athletes earned second-team honors, including Pittsford freshman Layla Bryner and sophomore Ellie Bump, Hillsdale Academy junior Abigail Kriesch and freshman Lucy Molenkamp and Camden-Frontier junior Alyssa Schroeder. Litchfield, Waldron and North Adams-Jerome were also represented among the honorable mention selections, with all six Hillsdale County programs competing in the division earning postseason recognition. title: Jacob Campsey's returns home and revives Devine's football program
summary: Jacob Campsey's returns home and revives Devine's football program with best playoff push since 2011.
content: Members of Devine's football team pose with a banner signifying the Warhorses' 2026 District 14-3A-I championship. (Courtesy/Jacob Campsey) Jacob Campsey proudly strode into San Antonio's Region 20 Education Service Center on Feb. 1 - his first day as Devine's head football coach and athletic director - for UIL's biennial realignment announcement. It was a big one for the Warhorses, who had changed classifications from 4A to 3A, and for Campsey, who was set to take charge at this alma mater 20 years after graduating from there. Everything was new and familiar at the same time. "I have such pride in this brand," Campsey said. "Anytime I put on the ‘DW,' my chest swells up, and that's the honest truth. I feel like the brand represents so many things that are positive in the world, and that's what I love about it." He believes that connection to Devine – a town of 4,700 located about 40 miles south of downtown San Antonio on I-35 - is a big reason why the Warhorses are in the third round of the playoffs for the first time since 2011. "He played for the same team, so I feel there was a better connection between him and the players because he went through all the same stuff we go through," junior running back Enoch Hall said. "He has the experience, and he knows what's right and what's wrong." Jacob Campsey, a 2006 Devine graduate, is in his first season leading his alma mater. The Warhorses are in the third round of the playoffs for the first time since 2011. (Courtesy/Jacob Campsey) Devine (11-1) faces reigning state champion Yoakum (10-2) in a Class 3A Division I regional semifinal at 7 p.m. Friday at Heroes Stadium. The Warhorses earned that opportunity with a come-from-behind victory against Orange Grove last week. Devine trailed by two touchdowns in the first half before staging a big second half for a 49-33 victory. The week before, Devine downed Randolph, 69-21, for its first playoff win since 2015. The Warhorses entered the postseason with 10 straight first round playoffs. "I think it really lit a fire under everybody after we won that first playoff game," junior receiver/defensive back Brody Lane said. "It kind of set everyone's eyes that we could actually go somewhere with this." The Warhorses' run is exactly how Campsey envisioned when he laid out his step-by-step plan to his players in February. Campsey, 38, was hired at Devine after serving as defensive coordinator for three years at Bandera. Campsey pursued the opportunity after Paul Gomez stepped down after nine seasons as Devine's head coach. "Obviously, being home and understanding what the program was about and the foundation that the program had, those opportunities don't come along very often," Campsey said. "It was one of those things that was a no-brainer for me." Before Bandera, Campsey was at Rockdale where he was head coach from 2020-2022 and prior to that, a defensive assistant from 2016-19. Campsey was Rockdale's defensive coordinator in 2017 when the Tigers won the Class 3A Division I state championship. "I had a little bit of an advantage because when you walk in with a state championship ring, there's an immediate buy-in," Campsey said. "They don't have to wonder if it's going to work. The biggest thing was I presented a plan – here are the steps, here's the roadmap , here's what it takes. Here's what we're going to do, and they did it." Devine quarterback Jacob Campsey moves to the outside as Hondo defender Tyler Graff pursues Friday in Hondo. HONDO DEVINE HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL TOM REEL/STAFF NOVEMBER 7, 2003. (TOM REEL/SAN ANTONIO EXPRESS-NEWS) During his playing days, Campsey was a varsity quarterback for Devine for three seasons beginning in 2003. In each of those seasons, the Warhorses when three rounds deep in the postseason. He attended college (but didn't play football) at Mary Hardin-Baylor and got his first assistant job at Thrall when he graduated. After three years there, he went to Rockdale. "Once the whole team saw that he had won a state title and he was really successful in the past few years, it made us all think we were really going to be good," Lane said. It wasn't an easy adjustment. The Warhorses, rooted in the Wishbone since Campsey's playing days, switched to the spread. It was still a run-based offense, but it places an emphasis on getting the ball to their athletes in space. Defensively, the Warhorses went away from a three-man front. Without the benefit of spring practice, the Warhorses made the most of their allotted time during athletic period when they were allowed to run football drills in T-shirts and shorts. They called it their "Breakfast Club" workouts where between 80 and 85 athletes showed up at 6:30 a.m. "That allowed us to get ahead of the curve on some things we were changing schematically," Campsey said. The Warhorses have benefited. Hall has rushed for 1,859 yards and 31 touchdowns on 221 carries. Sophomore Nathan Valle has passed for 2,045 yards and 29 touchdowns. Lane has caught 49 passes for 1,103 yards and 19 touchdowns. A season ago, Hall rushed for 1,329 yards and 18 touchdowns in 11 games. As a team, the Warhorses threw for 1,327 yards and 13 scores. After dropping its season opener against San Diego, 39-21, Devine has reeled off 11 straight wins. They haven't won 11 game in a season since 2011 when it went 13-1 and made it to the state quarterfinals. Devine went 7-0 in 14-3A-I to win its first district championship since 2022. "Everything was new and we definitely had to get used to it," Lane said. "From that first game against San Diego, we've really embraced it. Since that first loss, we've been going through everything with a great mindset that we really wanted to do this (get far in the playoffs) as a team." title: Miami basketball's Acaden Lewis is giving back through his charity Bucket Blessings
summary: Acaden Lewis looks back at the event as simple, but he recalls that it felt different than anything he’d done before. Lewis and his family members had always volunteered at soup kitchens, but they decided that the 2024 Thanksgiving season—when…
content: Acaden Lewis looks back at the event as simple, but he recalls that it felt different than anything he’d done before. Lewis and his family members had always volunteered at soup kitchens, but they decided that the 2024 Thanksgiving season—when Lewis was a high schooler—would be different. They were going to conduct their own event, not one that they were merely volunteering at. A family friend who owns a Halal food restaurant called Bites had supplied food free of charge to Lewis, his mom, his dad and his uncle to give out that night. So, they walked the streets of northeast Washington, D.C., passing it out to homeless people in the area. Lewis—Miami’s starting point guard, who averages 10.9 points per game and is referred to as a "basketball savant" by Miami coach Jai Lucas—helped plan the night and was instrumental in bringing it to fruition. All these years later, he still remembers how he felt at the end of that night and how he could tell the event impacted the “It was the first time I really saw the impact,” Lewis told Basket Under Review, “And what it could be.” That night was the first time Lewis’ non-profit charity, Bucket Blessings, was more than an idea. Bucket Blessings has since conducted over 10 events and has served over 500 children—as well as adults. The charity’s website outlines that it specializes in community building, youth empowerment and giving back through basketball training. Lewis is named as the charity's founder, and the website shows Lewis participating in all three aspects of the charity’s vision. Its mission statement declares that it empowers communities and inspires hope. That November night, Lewis realized that doing so with some level of consistency was possible. “I thought that was a great stepping stone,” Lewis said. “Since then, we really haven’t looked back. We’ve continued to do the same things, grow our platform, and keep helping people out. That first one just showed us the possibilities.” Lewis saw the possibilities for his charity through its first event, around Thanksgiving. (Miami Athletics) LEWIS WAS STARTING to pick up notoriety as a result of the combination of the awards he was winning, coverage he was garnering and the volume of high-major offers that were set to come his way. But Lewis’ parents, Nateya Pompeo and Jarrett Lewis, knew how those things change people. They weren’t going to let them. They were intent on making sure that he was thankful for everything he’d gotten. They wanted to make sure he stayed humble. They wanted him to appreciate his life and how fortunate he was. Lewis’ rise was about to accelerate significantly, and they could tell. So they threw around ideas for how they could keep instilling important values in his life. They landed on launching Bucket Blessings. “We were talking about it and were like, ‘We want to make sure that if things really take off for him, that he is centered on community and giving back and staying humble,” Nateya said. “That’s where it started, wanting to give him that foundation before the journey really took off.” Pompeo and Jarrett thought they could do that while also giving back to the large population in their Washington, D.C., community who had it harder than they did. So, they started the charity while Lewis was in high school and partnered with organizations, pouring their own money into it to get it off the ground while he had no income. They felt that was an example to Lewis, showing him what it should look like once he made his own money. It appears as if he’s taken their guidance to heart. Lewis, his parents and his uncle TJ Pompeo have since coordinated Thanksgiving food distribution—which has been Lewis’ favorite event—and have conducted basketball clinics for kids. Those clinics have featured Lewis working out with his trainers and coaches, as well as speeches from those coaches—who said success was possible for them, even without an abundance of resources. All the kids love when basketball is tied into the events, Nateya estimates. The events that stick out in Nateya’s mind the most are the trips to the Ronald McDonald House—which provides low-cost or free lodging, meals, and support near hospitals for families whose children are receiving medical treatment far from home. One was particularly fulfilling for her because it involved her friends, Lewis and his friends and Jarrett and his friends all cooking for the children in the house. But they think they may have topped their Ronald McDonald House events recently when they went to the Liberty City Elementary School in Miami. They surprised the kids with an ice cream truck, played basketball with them, held a Q&A with Lewis and his teammates, and met the school’s pressing need for toiletries—necessitated by the children having to clean up there. That day embodied the vision for Bucket Blessing. “The goal of the charity is to empower families that don’t really have as much economic status as they would like,” Lewis said. “Once we realized we had the opportunity because I had some NIL money and we had some things to fund it, we thought it’d be a great idea to give back.” Lewis has followed his parents' lead. (Miami Athletics) IT’S 6:00 A.M. on this June morning and Lewis is pounding the ball on the hardwood of the Rock Creek gym. Lewis knows this gym well, at least well enough to know that it doesn’t have heat in the winter or a strong air conditioning system in the summer. The circumstance is no longer jarring for Lewis. He’s played games on church-floor carpets. He’s run the show in a gym without bleachers because of the cost. Some gyms didn’t have enough basketballs for everyone to play, and they required Lewis’ family to donate equipment. He worked out in D.C. He worked out in Baltimore. The difference between those courts and the double-decker, lavish ones he played in with his high school was night and day. “I’ve been in all types of gyms,” Lewis said, “Whether they be nice, have a lot going on, AC, a lot of beautiful things around it and I’ve also been in some pretty trenchy ones. I think even that experience shows how the DMV and the D.C. area can be.” Lewis’ experience in every type of gym that his surroundings had to offer was a microcosm of his upbringing. It was also by design. "Be better, be different," Inside Shelton Henderson's rapid rise Nateya and Jarrett consider themselves fortunate to have been financially stable, but they didn’t want him to grow up in a bubble. Jarrett was raised in Detroit and lived in the inner city in some of the city’s worst times, while Nateya grew up in New York, where she developed a toughness and an awareness of people from all walks of life. Both families experienced financial struggles. Lewis’ parents talked about their backgrounds and decided that they didn’t want him to forget what was going on around him. As a result, they didn’t send him to private school until high school and encouraged him to have balance. “We knew it would help develop him to understand how different daily life is for a kid his age in one person’s shoes vs. another person’s,” Nateya said. “He still embodies so much of both of the worlds that he walks in.” Nateya clarifies. Lewis was in both environments nearly daily. He had friends in each. He consistently juggled both lifestyles and let each of them mold him. “He been in the heart of it the majority of his life,” Lewis’ longtime trainer Chris Howard said. When Lewis’ parents watch him speak these days, they feel affirmed that they couldn’t have made a better decision about the environments they chose for him. Lewis developed grit and fire from being in environments where not much was given. He also developed an appreciation for the significance of being in safe, well-resourced environments. “I got to see how people live within their means and also saw and got to experience within the schools a different side of life where people had more money, could afford more and live a certain lifestyle,” Lewis said. “I really got to see that everyone can live life differently and still enjoy their life and that it’s okay to ask for help.” Lewis reflects that being around kids and families who didn’t have much made him realize his problems weren’t as big as he thought. It was easy for him to wish he had more, but he realized there were plenty of families who wished they had the bare minimum and would quickly trade their situations for his. Lewis had two parents, a house to live in, food on his plate and enough clothes. He realized through his upbringing that not everyone has that. Lewis tends to agree with his parents that where he was raised was advantageous in his development as a person, so much so that he will bring his future kids to his home community one day–and isn’t ruling out raising them there. He still wears D.C. on his sleeve–literally, with the U.S. Capitol building and a tribute to Trinidad, his father’s home area. “Acaden definitely embodies the DMV,” Howard–who declares that Lewis was raised right by Jarrett and Nateya–said. “He has that hunger and that mindset.” Lewis has seen all areas of the DMV. (Miami Athletics) LEWIS LEFT HIS HIGH-TOP CHAIR , fist-bumped Miami wing Shelton Henderson and walked across the stage towards the podium at ACC Media Days. Before he could greet the crowd of reporters on hand, the moderator prompted him with a question. The moderator brought up that Lewis had started Bucket Blessings in 2024 and wanted Lewis to share more with the room before moving on to basketball questions–which there were plenty of, considering Lewis’ offseason transfer from Villanova to Miami. Lewis explained that he saw both good and bad in the area where he grew up, which prompted him and his parents to start the charity. He then went down the list of events that the charity has conducted. A reporter then followed up and asked why Lewis has chosen to be involved the way he has. His answer? Why not. “He is just really unbelievable for a kid that age to understand how much this means to others. “Just him showing up, shaking hands, talking with the kids,” Nateya said. “I watch it with my own two eyes and I get a little teary-eyed about it because they are so excited to be around him. You can’t put a price tag on that.” Lewis believes it’s an entirely different feeling to directly help someone than it is to impact them through his play. He considers giving back his way of returning the favor for the positive infrastructure he was surrounded by growing up. Those close to Lewis believe he means what he says. By all accounts, Lewis never tells his family that he can’t fit an event or is too busy to plan one. They say he’s always willing to help, and that he’s made it a clear priority to do things that mean something to others. They think that says something about him. He believes that’s his duty. “You’re not as inconvenienced as you think,” Lewis said. “You have two hours of your day to go help out whether you won or lost the game, or you have somewhere to go the next day. You have two hours to help out someone that’s in a way worse situation than you.”

title: South Jersey 2026 Thanksgiving high school football roundup
summary: A roundup of 2026 Thanksgiving high school football action across South Jersey
content: This story will be updated as scores are reported. Wednesday, Nov. 25 Atlantic City 45, Holy Spirit 6: Ahmad Chambers had four touchdowns as the Vikings sprinted away on the 98 th edition against their traditional rivals. Chambers started the scoring with a two-yard, first quarter scoring plunge. Later, the back added an 80-yard run followed immediately by a 60-yard interception return in the third quarter and a 20-yard score in the fourth. Marvin Burroughs and Don’Taye Thompson figured in two touchdowns each. Thompson caught a 13-yard pass from Burroughs, then turned a direct snap into a 25-yard TD run. Burroughs closed out the scoring with a 39-yard TD pass to Kenai Austin. It was the 33 rd touchdown pass of the season for Burroughs. Johnny Varallo rolled around right end for a 10-yard score that briefly brought the Spartans to within one score early in the second quarter. The Spartans ended their season at 5-6. The Vikings were 9-4 this fall and lead the all-time series 54-40-4. Clayton 46, Pitman 0: Haven Walls returned the opening kickoff 82 yards and the Clippers sailed to a win in the 101 st Thanksgiving week edition of the rivalry. Naeem Smith scored a pair of first-half touchdowns from 13, then 12 yards. Anthony Briscoe turned a deflected pass into a 68-yard interception return. Willie Weathers scored from five yards out and Enok Figueroa closed out the half with a 32-yard score. After the break, Michael Bull scored on a 20-yard jaunt around right end. Pitman ended its season with a 4-6 mark while Clayton finished 7-3 for the season and closed the Panthers ’ lead in the series to 63-34-4. Paul VI 57, Camden Catholic 12: Sean DiNunzio threw three touchdown passes and Nate Klecko scored three times on the ground before halftime as the Eagles won the 59 th edition of the Turkey week rivalry. Klecko had finishing runs of one, five and 58 yards while compiling 269 on just 16 carries. DiNunzio opened the night with a 32-yard pass to Kevin Bunt, then added a 19-yard strike to Iyon Townsend and a 39-yard connection with Tommy Dromgoole before halftime. Marcel Maynard closed out the evening with a seven-yard TD run. Nymir Daily scored twice of the Irish, on a 47-yard, second quarter run and from 10 yards out in the fourth. Camden Catholic saw its record even out at 5-5. The Eagles are 5-4 on the season and cut into the Irish lead in the series to 32-26-1. Thanksgiving Audubon 29, Haddon Township 0: Green Wave senior lineman Nate Witts barreled into the line for a three-yard, second quarter touchdown to turn his first career carry into a touchdown in the 63 rd and final Curley Cup meeting to be held on Thanksgiving. Earlier, Michael DeLuca scored on a 19-yard, first-quarter pass from Jude Cotter. Michael Aversa added an eight-yard touchdown run and Nolan Figueroa scored from nine in the second half. The Hawks concluded their season with a 3-6 mark. The Green Wave was 7-3 this fall and extended their advantage in the Curley Cup to 45-17-1. Millville 17, Vineland 0: Jahcere Graves scored the only touchdown of the first half as the Thunderbolts survived a soggy 155th edition of South Jersey’s oldest Thanksgiving rivalry, which dates to 1893. Millville claimed the Torny Surace/John Pierantozzi Cup for the 10 th consecutive season. Graves bulled in from a yard out on Millville’s third try after earning a first-and-goal from the 1. The ‘Bolts took advantage of the sloppy conditions with a safety after an errant punt snap squirted over the end line and turning a late fumble into a 27-yard Jack Powers field goal. Nyshon Jones continued Millville’s trend of taking advantage of the conditions, scooping up a fumble for an 18-yard touchdown in the third quarter. The Fighting Clan saw their record even out at 5-5. The Thunderbolts increased their lead in the Granddaddy of Them All to 69-67-19, and finished 7-5 for the year. Friday, Nov. 27 Haddon Heights at Haddonfield, 11 a.m. Saturday, Nov. 28 Camden at Eastside, 11 a.m. Tom Rimback grew up reading the Burlington County Times and Courier-Post sports sections and began writing for the BCT in 1996. He has covered everything from Super Bowls and Final Fours to Tri-County Swimming but he’s happiest on a sideline interviewing South Jersey scholastic athletes for the Courier-Post, Burlington County Times and Daily Journal. Follow him on twitter @Rimbacksports. Email him with story ideas at tomrimback@gmail.com and, most importantly, support local journalism with a subscription. title: Super 25 football schedule: Thanksgiving weekend's biggest high school games
summary: See when and where the USA TODAY Sports Super 25 high school football teams play in Week 15, with state titles on the line over Thanksgiving weekend.
content: The high school football playoffs continue across the country, with many states hosting championships this Thanksgiving weekend. Fans across the country hope to be spoiled with more upsets, as the top teams in the country play each other and create a ripple effect in the Super 25 rankings. Which teams are on upset alert? Here's when and where each USA TODAY Sports Super 25 team is scheduled to play this week. 1. Buford (GA) Friday, Nov. 27, at Valdosta (GA), 7 p.m. ET A couple of hours after the Wolves beat Archer (GA) in a blowout 42-6 win, the door cracked open for Buford to take the No. 1 spot in the Super 25 rankings as Santa Margarita (CA) fell. Valdosta is coming off a 38-31 win over East Coweta (GA). 2. Allen (TX) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Odessa Permian (TX), 6 p.m. CT Allen has outscored its opponents 117-0 in the playoffs following a 44-0 win over Trinity (TX). Now, the Eagles face their toughest test to date when they play Odessa Permian, which is also 12-0 and coming off a 41-15 win over Keller (TX). 3. IMG Academy (Bradenton, FL) Season completed 4. North Crowley (Fort Worth, TX) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. College Park (TX), 7 p.m. CT The Panthers scored at least 40 points for the 10th time in 12 games this season, winning 49-14 over North Forney (TX) to remain unbeaten. College Park (9-3) is coming off a close 28-21 win over Langham Creek (TX). 5. St. Thomas Aquinas (Fort Lauderdale, FL) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Chaminade-Madonna (FL), 7 p.m. ET Bouncing back from a disappointing overtime loss to Lakeland (FL), the Raiders rolled past Venice (FL) 38-16 to remain alive in the Open Division pool play. Meanwhile, Chaminade-Madonna is coming off a 28-27 loss to Lakeland and also needs a win to keep its season alive. 6. Columbus (Miami, FL) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. West Boca Raton (FL), 3 p.m. ET A pair of 11-1 teams face off in a matchup that could determine Pool B semifinal seeding, with both teams 2-0 in Open Division Pool B play. The Bulls are coming off a 21-10 win over Miami Central, while the Explorers beat Raines 28-6. 7. Bishop Gorman (Las Vegas, NV) Idle 8. Baylor (Chattanooga, TN) Idle 9. Carrollton (GA) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. North Gwinnett (GA), 7:30 p.m. ET Carrollton escaped Parkview (GA) with a 41-33 win last week, trailing in the fourth quarter but pulling out the win. North Gwinnett is fresh off a 35-28 win over Westlake. 10. St. John Bosco (Bellflower, CA) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Centennial (CA), 7 p.m. PT In the preseason Super 25 , St. John Bosco and Centennial were No. 2 and No. 5, respectively. Now they play for the CIF-SS championship. The Braves are fresh off a 27-2 win over Santa Margarita, while the Huskies took down Sierra Canyon, 42-19. 11. De La Salle (Concord, CA) Idle 12. Centennial (Corona, CA) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. St. John Bosco (CA), 7 p.m. PT In the preseason Super 25 , St. John Bosco and Centennial were No. 2 and No. 5, respectively. Now they play for the CIF-SS championship. The Braves are fresh off a 27-2 win over Santa Margarita, while the Huskies took down Sierra Canyon, 42-19. 13. Brownsburg (IN) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Penn (IN), 7 p.m. ET Brownsburg puts its 32-game winning streak on the line against a Penn program that has won 13 straight as the teams fight for a state championship. The matchup between quarterbacks Landon Hall and Oscar Frye will be a key matchup to watch. 14. Lakeland (FL) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Venice (FL), 7:30 p.m. ET With wins over St. Thomas Aquinas (27-24) and Chaminade-Madonna (28-27), Lakeland is 2-0 in Open Division pool play and on to the semifinals, while Venice is 0-2 and eliminated. But don't expect the Dreadnaughts to take the week off. 15. The St. James Academy (Springfield, VA) Idle 16. Thomas County Central (Thomasville, GA) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Creekside (GA), 7:30 p.m. ET With these teams matching up in the quarterfinals, it marks just the fifth time in GHSA playoff history that two defending champions will square off. Thomas County Central has won 18 straight, while Creekside is on an 11-game winning streak. Something will have to give. 17. Santa Margarita (Rancho Santa Margarita, CA) Season completed 18. Hough (Cornelius, NC) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Chambers (NC), 7 p.m. ET These two teams square off following vastly different third-round games. Hough dominated for a 63–21 win vs. West Forsyth, while Chambers is coming off a 15-8 win over Mallard Creek. The Huskies have 10 wins by more than 25 points this year. 19. Sierra Canyon (Chatsworth, CA) Season completed 20. Trinity (Louisville, KY) Friday, Nov. 27, at Frederick Douglass (KY), 6 p.m. ET Breaking: Someone finally scored on Trinity, ending the Shamrocks' eight-game shutout streak. However, they still pulled out the 48-9 win. The Broncos are fresh off a 42-7 win over Simon Kenton. 21. C.E. King (Houston, TX) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Ridge Point (TX), 2 p.m. CT C.E. King rolls in off a 62-18 win in the area round, pushing its winning streak to 11 straight games. Ridge Point is 12-0 and has won every single game this year by at least 12 points. 22. Central Catholic (Pittsburgh, PA) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. State College (PA), 7 p.m. ET Central Catholic (11-0) and State College (13-0) face off in a matchup of unbeaten teams, so something will have to give. The Vikings defeated the Lions 42-21 in the 6A quarterfinals. 23. Tupelo (MS) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Germantown (MS), 7 p.m. CT Tupelo takes on Germantown in its first North State championship game in school history. The winner advances to the MHSAA Class 7A championship game. The Golden Wave are coming off a 42-7 win over Madison Central. 24. Bishop Watterson (Columbus, OH) Friday, Nov. 27, vs. Nordonia (OH), 7 p.m. ET Bishop Watterson dominated Massillon for a 22-5 win last week, the 12th game of the season allowing fewer than 13 points. The Eagles have won nine straight following a 23-21 loss to Highland on Sept. 11. 25. Liberty (Peoria, AZ) Saturday, Nov. 28, vs. Basha (AZ), 6 p.m. MT Two of the top teams in Arizona face off in the AIA Open Division Football semifinals with a trip to the state championship game on the line. The Bears handed the Lions their lone loss, 30-22, on Sept. 18. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Super 25 football schedule: Thanksgiving weekend's biggest high school games

title: 3 quick takeaways from Wisconsin’s win over Northeastern: The bench provides a spark
summary: The Badgers played a clean game in a big win over Northeastern.
content: Hayden Jones #13 of the Wisconsin Badgers shoots while defended by Petar Pinter #13 of the Northeastern Huskies at the Kohl Center in Madison, Wisconsin, United States, on November 25, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Wisconsin Badgers blew past the Northeastern Huskies 91-54 on Wednesday evening, securing a much-needed win as they improved to 5-2 on the season. Wisconsin had a disappointing week at the Baha Mar Championship last weekend. Now returning home against Northeastern, the Badgers were notable favorites, with the spread being at 20.5 points ahead of tip-off. But Wisconsin had seen their struggles as big favorites against non-conference teams so far this season. Three of their four wins were by single digits, despite the Badgers being favored by over 20 points in those games. So, there were some question marks for the team going into Wednesday night. But Wisconsin shrugged those off and blew out Northeastern, kicking off Thanksgiving on a good note. Here are three quick takeaways from the Badgers 91-54 win over Northeastern. Starting lineup change Wisconsin made two changes in the starting lineup, replacing Eian Elmer with freshman Jackson Ball and Victory Onuetu with Austin Rapp. Ball’s start was short-lived as he suffered a lower-body injury, playing just two minutes on the night. But Rapp was the team’s leading scorer with 14 points, hitting four threes in his first start of the season. Rapp had already been playing starter-like minutes. The ripple effect was seen more elsewhere in the rotation. Wisconsin gave Onuetu just three first-half minutes, while Will Garlock was their main center off the bench. Garlock had 12 points, eight rebounds, and six assists in 25 minutes. Onuetu has struggled to start the season, so it’s not a surprise his role has diminished so far. But Wisconsin will need Garlock to continue being a quality contributor off the bench with their depth. With Ball’s injury, Elmer was thrust back into early minutes, and it was a similar story. He finished with seven points in 22 minutes, but it still feels like he’s struggling to find his impact on this team. Assertiveness has been a common issue for him so far, but he’s talented enough to find his way. Let’s see if the lineup change sparks that. Bench shows up Without Jack Janicki, the Badgers needed other bench players to show up on Wednesday, and they got that. Hayden Jones provided the spark with 13 points on 5-for-7 shooting, ranking second on the team behind Austin Rapp. He earned praise from Greg Gard after the game for how he responded with his minutes. As mentioned above, Garlock had another quality game as well, while shooting 100 percent from the field. Zach Kinziger didn’t have the best shooting night, but he dished out four assists in 19 minutes while committing zero turnovers. Even Trey Autry had eight second-half points. Wisconsin had 49 bench points in the win, making up more than 50 percent of its scoring. It was a good day for the bench on Wednesday. Protecting the ball A huge issue for the Badgers in the Baha Mar Championship was turnovers. Wisconsin had a brutal 18 turnovers against Seton Hall in a five-point loss, and then committed 17 in the blowout loss to Murray State. Well, they fixed that on Wednesday, committing just five turnovers as they averaged a stellar 1.4 points per possession. A big part of that goes to point guards Owen Foxwell and Zach Kinziger, who combined for 12 assists and zero turnovers. On the flip side, they forced 12 from Northeastern, resulting in 19 points off turnovers. The defense was on point, holding the Huskies to 35 percent from the field and 21.7 percent from three, while the offense was efficient and played clean.

title: ACC Roundup – Comebacks And Strangeness Abound
summary: Strange night around the ACC
content: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - NOVEMBER 13: Pittsburgh Panthers forward Baye Ndongo (11) grabs a loose ball during the men's college basketball game between the Butler Bulldogs and Pittsburgh Panthers on November 13, 2026, at Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In Wednesday’s ACC Action, Virginia got by Marquette, 60-54, Syracuse bit down on Albany, 74-53, NC State walloped Norfolk State, 80-49, SMU got hammered by Utah State, 93-59, Wake Forest got by Mississippi State, 78-71, Stanford was nipped by Saint Louis, 66-64, while Clemson fell short against Colorado State, 77-75. If you haven’t heard, the ballroom at Atlantis where they hold that tournament has been having major problems with water leakage, and in Virginia’s case, the delay was 95 minutes. The final score of 60-54 was more of a Tony Bennett-type outcome, but you’ll never get things exactly the way you want. We’re sure Ryan Odom is happy with a win, even if he had to get outside his comfort zone to get it. It’s the mark of a good coach, actually. We’ve never thought that Shaka Smart was that great at that, but he adapted well, too. In the end, Virginia survived 13 first-half turnovers and falling behind by 21-11 early. After the rather lengthy halftime, Virginia’s defense proved sturdier, and the Cavs won even after Thijs De Ridder fouled out with 4:49 to play. In short, lots of adversity in this game, but Virginia overcame it. Props to the Cavs as Odom wins the battle of the former VCU coaches. Syracuse and Albany were tied at the half, but in the second, the Orange blew the game open, winning that half 48-26. Amusingly, Gerry McNamara had to go to the 2-3 zone. Both McNamara and his predecessor, Adrian Autry, prefer man-to-man, but Jim Boeheim’s staple defense still gets hauled out from time to time. We saw some highlights in an earlier game and freshman Ryan Moesch really jumped out at us. He started here, and nearly had a triple-double with 13 points, 9 rebounds, and 8 assists. He also had 4 steals. Quite a game for the rook. This was good prep for Syracuse’s matchup with Oklahoma in the upcoming ACC/SEC Challenge. We haven’t looked closely at the matchups, but Syracuse has a shot. NC State had an easy night against Norfolk State. Paul McNeil had 20 points, while big man Zymicah Wilkins had 15 points and 8 rebounds. Wilkins, a redshirt freshman, and Kingston Whitty started the second half for State. In the first half, both teams got 19 boards each, but after the half, State took over, winning the rebounding battle, 25-10. With the win, State moves to 6-1, but the schedule is pretty weak. We’ll get a better idea of how the Pack is doing soon. The SMU blowout surprised us, until we remembered that former Northern Iowa coach Ben Jacobson took that job: mystery solved. That guy is a heck of a coach. SMU was just awful: the starters only scored 24 points. Meanwhile, the Aggies shot 53.8 percent from deep and 56.9 percent overall. That suggests dreadful defense too. Utah State was up by 38 points at one point. Just a terrible, terrible outing by the Mustangs. It’s pretty clear that Wake’s Steve Forbes can coach; his problem has been getting enough talent to show it. He may have a decent group this year. Freshman center Gavin Placide is averaging 15.8 ppg and 7.8 rebounds. Justin Ray and Kevair Kennedy have had their moments as well. Wake had a nice first-half 11-0 run, fueled by forcing six turnovers, and controlled the boards, 39-24, against a good rebounding team. It was a competitive game, but in the end, the Deacs shut the Bulldogs down for three minutes late, and shot 10-10 from the line down the stretch run. Placide Daily Double: Gavin and twin Gallagher Placide combined for 23 points and 14 rebounds. Clemson has played three games in the Maui Classic, and in all three, they dug huge first-half holes they nearly dug themselves out of. Nearly, but all three times they came up short. The Tigers were down 24 to Ole Miss, 10 to Washington, and 27 to Colorado State. Actually, it’s a stretch to say that Clemson almost dug out of it against Ole Miss, but they were competitive in the second half. Against Washington, they lost by one point, and against Colorado State, they lost by two. It’s bound to be a frustrating pattern for Brad Brownell: clearly, his team can compete, but it hasn’t mastered competing for the entire game. As noted against Washington, Ace Buckner had to do too much. He got more help here, as Chase Thompson and David Fuchs both got 19 points, but Dylan Faulkner and Cole Certa each shot 2-7. Faulkner finished with 7 points, while Certa got 10. Buckner shot 5-17. If he were able to play to his strengths, he’d be much more efficient. Finally, Stanford took Saint Louis to the wire before losing 66-64. Stanford didn’t shoot well, but stayed in the game with 9 made threes and with 15 points off turnovers. That made up 42 of Stanford’s 64 points. Toss in 11 from the line, and that’s 53. But the Cardinal shot just 65 percent from the line (11-17), and might have won the game with just a few more points from the line. Freshman guard Julius Price racked up 31 points, while fellow freshmen Aziz Olajuwon got 14. The other three starters combined for just 11 points. Thanksgiving Day will be surprisingly good, with Boston College taking on Johnny Dawkins’ UCF, Miami playing a struggling Washington, a hopefully angry SMU taking on LSU, undefeated DePaul taking on undefeated Pitt, and Louisville in the nightcap with St. John’s. Do you think Rick Pitino will be fired up to play his old school? Maybe just a bit. content: The Hawaii men’s basketball team had the final word. Down by as many as 13 and never leading in regulation, the Rainbow Warriors rallied for an 83-81 overtime victory over Incarnate Word at Bankoh Arena at Stan Sheriff Center. Bol Dengbit demonstrated his skills from near and far to lift the ’Bows to their fourth win in six games this season. The Cardinals fell to 1-6, with all their losses against Division I opponents. But the visitors from San Antonio gave the ’Bows fits with their athleticism, switching defenses and guard play. Jayden Thomas scored 19 points and Ismail Habib, a transfer from Division II Southern Indiana, added a season-high 18 for the Cardinals. The ’Bows took advantage of the Cardinals’ foul troubles to score 10 of the first 12 points of the second half. Incarnate Word committed six fouls in first 3:35 of the second half. UIW starters Godswill Erheriene, a left-handed rim protector, and Krisnan-Cole Ioane each were assessed their fourth fouls during that stretch. The ’Bows trailed 69-66 when point guard Jalem Matingou fed the 6-11 Dengdit on the right wing. Dengdit’s 3 was true, tying it at 69 with 11 seconds left in regulation. Matingou’s free throw to open the extra period gave the ’Bows their first lead of the game. Matingou scored the ’Bows’first five points of overtime, making it 74-69, before fouling out. The Cardinals closed to 82-81 on Brandon McCreesh’s two free throws with 6 seconds left. It was 83-81 after Chance Trujillo’s free throw with 4 seconds left. The Cardinals set up for the dramatic finish. But Max Garcia-Plata missed a 3 as time expired. In a sequence that encapsulated the ’Bows’ woes, Manie Joses missed a hooked, grabbed the rebound, and missed the putback as time expired in the first half. The Cardinals were able to use a divide-and-conquer method to take a 36-25 lead into the intermission. The Cardinals would widen their attack, setting up an isolation into the lane. That led to close-up shots or kickout to the wings. Ismael Habib, wearing a face mask, led the Cardinals with 12 first-half points — six coming on two 3s. Point guard Mekhi Connor, who averaged more than six assists per game during his career, picked up his third foul with 6:27 left in the first half. But Habib and Jayden Thomas were able to steer the Cardinals’ offense. The ’Bows tried different rotations. Forward Zack Davidson, who entered as their leading scorer, came off the bench in a time-sharing role with Dengdit at the five position. After missing the first five games because of an ankle injury, Joses made his UH debut. London-reared Joses started. While he provided solid defense, he endured rusty shooting. He missed all six of his first-half shots. Despite finishing with five points, Joses, who has a 71-inch wing span, helped UH’s defense. Davidson scored his 20 points in the second half. Davidson also hit six of six free throws. Dengdit, a transfer from UC San Diego, finished with 24 points and 13 rebounds. Matingou had 20 points. The ’Bows missed 14 of 16 free throws and 13 layup attempts. But Dendit, who made 25 3-point shots with UCSD last season, made the ones that counted most. title: Clemson storms back, fails to finish job in loss against Colorado State
summary: Brad Brownell and the Clemson men’s basketball team dropped a close on on Wednesday to Colorado State.
content: Clemson had a chance to take the lead with 26 seconds left against Colorado State , a scenario that would have been hard to imagine at halftime. David Fuchs’ 3-pointer from the left corner caught the back rim, and the Rams used the final possession to hand the Tigers their third loss in Maui. Jojo McIver drove from the right wing and floated a shot that bounced in as time expired, giving Colorado State a 77-75 win at the Lahaina Civic Center. The loss dropped Clemson to 4-4 and left Brad Brownell’s team in last place in the eight-team Maui Invitational field. The Tigers spent most of the second half digging out of a hole that took Colorado State just minutes to build. The Rams went on a 17-0 run in the first half and made 14 consecutive shots at one point, taking a 55-28 lead into the break. Clemson held Colorado State scoreless for the first 7:45 of the second half and scored 18 straight points to get back in the game. Ace Buckner eventually tied it at 65 with a jumper, and Fuchs put the Tigers in front with a free throw with 5:05 remaining. It was Clemson’s first lead since the opening minutes. The Rams pulled ahead 75-70 with 2:02 left, only for Clemson to score the next five points and tie it again inside the final minute. The Tigers had one more look at the lead before McIver ended it. Dabo Swinney is enjoying his time with Clemson team, despite struggles 📸 Rich Barnes, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect https://t.co/4G5BOXR3Oy pic.twitter.com/NevYpnUqfp — Clemson Wire (@Clemson_Wire) November 25, 2026 Chase Thompson and Fuchs each scored 19 points for Clemson. Thompson went 7-for-8 from the field and made all four of his 3-point attempts, while Fuchs grabbed nine rebounds. Buckner added 16 points and eight rebounds. Clemson returns to Littlejohn Coliseum on Tuesday, Dec. 1, to host Auburn in the ACC/SEC Challenge. Tipoff is set for 7 p.m. ET on ESPNU. title: Jalen Shelley emerging as Texas A&M basketball's clutch performer
summary: Jalen Shelley continues delivering in clutch situations for Texas A&M, but the Aggies' loss to Xavier highlighted the need for Cade Phillips.
content: Despite suffering its first loss of the season Wednesday against Xavier, Texas A&M basketball continues to learn a lot about its roster. One of the more encouraging developments has been the emergence of Jalen Shelley as a reliable option in late-game situations. While PJ Haggerty has received much of the attention for his offensive production , Shelley has shown over the last two games that he can deliver when the Aggies need a basket. Against TCU, the Loyola Marymount transfer scored eight of his 19 points in overtime, knocking down two crucial 3-pointers before recording a game-sealing steal. Shelley nearly delivered another comeback victory against Xavier, finishing with 16 points, two rebounds, two assists, two blocks and two steals. The versatile forward recorded two dunks in less than a minute during Texas A&M's second-half comeback before knocking down a 3-pointer to tie the game at 83 with 37 seconds remaining. Although the Aggies ultimately fell 88-83 , having another player capable of creating his own shot in late-game situations should take some pressure off Haggerty moving forward. However, Wednesday's loss also highlighted how much Texas A&M needs Cade Phillips back in the lineup . The Aggies were outrebounded 50-32, surrendered 17 offensive rebounds and had 10 shots blocked. Zach Clemence has done an admirable job filling in, and freshman Josh Irving continues to develop, but Phillips provides a physical interior presence that Texas A&M is currently missing. There is plenty to like about Bucky McMillan's team through seven games. Shelley's emergence as a clutch performer is another reason for optimism, but getting Phillips healthy could be critical to the Aggies' success once they enter the physical grind of SEC play. title: Michigan State Could Be Walking Into a Thanksgiving Upset Against Arkansas as 5.5 Point Underdogs
summary: DETROIT — No. 11 Michigan State (5-1) will have another difficult test on Thanksgiving Day. This time, the Spartans must contend with an Arkansas team capable of making things uncomfortable. The Arkansas Razorbacks (4-2) will meet the Spartans at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit. Tipoff is scheduled for 4:30 p.m. ET on CBS. On paper, Michigan State enters as the favorite. However, Arkansas has enough…
content: Nov 17, 2026; New York, New York, USA; Arkansas Razorbacks head coach John Calipari at Madison Square Garden. Mandatory Credit: Wendell Cruz-Imagn Images DETROIT — No. 11 Michigan State (5-1) will have another difficult test on Thanksgiving Day. This time, the Spartans must contend with an Arkansas team capable of making things uncomfortable. The Arkansas Razorbacks (4-2) will meet the Spartans at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit. Tipoff is scheduled for 4:30 p.m. ET on CBS. On paper, Michigan State enters as the favorite. However, Arkansas has enough offensive talent to make this a considerably closer matchup. Arkansas Has Plenty of Offensive Firepower Head coach John Calipari has assembled a young roster with considerable scoring potential. The Razorbacks are averaging 83.5 points through their first six games. Three players have established themselves as particularly important offensive contributors. Billy Richmond III leads Arkansas with 15.0 points per game, followed by Jeremiah Wilkinson at 14.7. Freshman guard Davion Thompson has also emerged as an important piece. He averages 11.3 points and 6.5 assists per game. Thompson recently delivered 13 points and 11 assists against Mississippi Valley State. His ability to create opportunities could become particularly important against Michigan State’s experienced backcourt. Meanwhile, Wilkinson is coming off an impressive shooting performance. He buried eight 3-pointers and finished with 28 points in Arkansas’ 92-48 victory. The Razorbacks have also shown they can compete against quality opposition. They pushed Indiana to an 81-76 finish before falling short on Nov. 17. Michigan State Has Its Own Challenges Michigan State has already demonstrated why it belongs among the country’s best teams. The Spartans defeated then-No. 2 Duke, 79-73, in the Champions Classic. However, Tom Izzo’s team suffered a 61-46 defeat against Tennessee. That performance exposed some offensive concerns heading into Thanksgiving. The Spartans responded with a 91-70 victory over Detroit Mercy. Jeremy Fears Jr. recorded 17 points and 14 assists in the win. Fears has been one of college basketball’s most productive floor generals. He averages 16.7 points and 9.3 assists per game. That presents a difficult assignment for Arkansas. Containing Fears and limiting his ability to create opportunities will be critical. Michigan State also has a considerable advantage on the glass. The Spartans rank among the nation’s better rebounding teams and have consistently generated second-chance opportunities. Arkansas cannot afford to give Michigan State extra possessions. That could quickly turn a competitive game into a comfortable Spartans victory. Calipari Knows What Awaits Him There is also some familiarity between these programs. Calipari and Izzo have developed a longstanding relationship through their coaching careers. Michigan State defeated Arkansas 69-66 in East Lansing last November. The Razorbacks will have an opportunity to return the favor in a much different environment. Calipari knows the physical challenge that comes with playing Izzo’s teams. “You’re playing Michigan State, it’s going to be roughhouse basketball,” Calipari told CBS Sports’ Jon Rothstein. That assessment could define Thursday’s matchup. Arkansas must match Michigan State’s physicality while maintaining its offensive rhythm. The Razorbacks also enter with a young roster. Handling adversity against an experienced opponent will be another important test. Michigan State could receive a boost from the expected returns of Coen Carr and Jordan Scott. Both starters missed the Spartans’ most recent game with injuries. Izzo said he expected both players to return against Arkansas. However, their availability and potential workloads remained dependent on their recovery. An Opportunity for an Arkansas Statement Arkansas has lost both of its matchups against high-major competition this season. Those defeats came against Virginia and Indiana. Consequently, Thursday represents an important opportunity for Calipari’s program. Beating a top-15 opponent would provide an early-season statement. Michigan State certainly has the experience and defensive discipline to avoid an upset. Still, Arkansas has enough offensive production to challenge the Spartans. The Razorbacks will need strong performances from Richmond, Wilkinson and Thompson. They must also limit turnovers and compete on the offensive glass. A victory would give Arkansas one of its most meaningful results of the young season. It would also give the program momentum heading into its upcoming SEC-ACC Challenge matchup against North Carolina. Michigan State and Arkansas meet Thursday, Nov. 26, at 4:30 p.m. ET. The Thanksgiving showdown will air nationally on CBS.

title: Purdue basketball introduces new starting lineup vs Oklahoma
summary: After a lackluster showing in Tuesday's loss to DePaul, Purdue has a new starting lineup for its Thanksgiving day game against Oklahoma.
content: FORT MYERS, Florida − After a 4-3 start to the season and after Tuesday's lackluster showing, Purdue basketball is introducing a new starting lineup. The Boilermakers will start a lineup consisting of Antione West Jr., Luke Ertel, Gicarri Harris, Jack Benter and Daniel Jacobsen against Oklahoma.
