title: Ten for Ten, Week 4: Grateful Gophers
summary: Five teams remain undefeated, while the losses keep coming for Purdue, Maryland and Michigan.
content: Ten for Ten is a weekly Big Ten basketball column. Every week, Adam and Donovan will discuss 10 of the biggest questions buzzing around the league and keep tabs on the conference’s best players, coaches and teams. Happy Turkey Day, folks! Though we’re just a month into the college basketball season, we’ve had such a fun time sharing our thoughts about Big Ten basketball every week with our loyal readers. We are grateful for all of our Ten for Ten readers and can’t wait for what’s to come with this column in the new year. On that note, what better way to celebrate America’s holiday than by talking about Feast Week college hoops? It’s Ten for Ten, Thanksgiving edition. Weekly ballot 1. Who was your team of the week? Adam: Iowa The Hawkeyes got off to a rough start to the season, dropping early games to Virginia Tech and Creighton, but they seemingly found a rhythm this past week. On Friday, they handed Xavier (No. 50 on KenPom.com ) its first loss of the season, pummeling the Musketeers for an 18-point victory. Then, on Tuesday, Iowa squashed UMBC 87-48, picking up its most lopsided win of the season. While head coach Ben McCollum doesn’t have an All-Big Ten, Bennett Stirtz-type offensive player on his squad this year, a multitude of Hawkeyes are stepping up to fill the void Stirtz left. The result has been a balanced offensive attack that actually grades out better than last year’s Elite Eight Iowa team. The Hawkeyes, who are currently KenPom.com’s No. 12-ranked offense, have five players averaging over eight points per game and have had different leading scorers in each of its last three games. Against Xavier, junior guard Isaia Howard logged a career-high 24 points and versus UMBC it was Cooper Koch that led the way, dropping 17. Don’t look now, but McCollum is starting to put the pieces together at the heart of the cornfields. Donovan: Minnesota Look at the Golden Gophers go. Head coach Niko Medved has Minneapolis hopping as his squad is off to one of the best starts in program history. Minnesota dismantled Oklahoma State and Utah in two 15-point high-major wins over the course of three days last weekend. Minnesota is now the 20th-ranked team in the country according to KenPom.com, directly ahead of Alabama, USC and Tennessee. It was a dreamy trip to the Shriners Children’s Charleston Classic, as the Golden Gophers announced themselves as a legitimate conference foe in the past seven days. 2. Who was your player of the week? Adam: Justin Pippen (Ohio State) Illinois freshman guard Quentin Coleman had the best single-game performance this week, but we’ve been talking too much about Illinois players as of late, so I decided to spread the love. Junior guard Justin Pippen, a California transfer and the son of NBA legend Scottie Pippen, has had a very solid start to his season in Columbus and just had his best week of the season, posting good performances against UMBC and No. 14 Vanderbilt. Across the two games, Pippen averaged 19.5 points, 5.0 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 2.0 steals, while shooting 13-for-21 (61.9%) from the field and 9-for-15 (60%) from the perimeter. The Buckeye is stepping into his own as one of the Big Ten’s most impactful point guards and will be an important piece for Jake Diebler’s squad come Big Ten play. Donovan: Quentin Coleman (Illinois) It seems like every week I’m praising this Illinois team, but Coleman’s performance on Monday was jaw-dropping. He scored 35 points on 12-for-18 shooting from the field while also tallying seven rebounds and six assists in the Fighting Illini’s win over Winthrop. Illinois’ 133 points were the program’s most ever in a single game and a Big Ten record. That came after the Illini scored 114 against Eastern Illinois. Now, it’s fair to ask why Brad Underwood’s bunch is playing two teams with a combined record of 1-13 over the course of a week, but let’s just focus on the freshman phenom. Coleman is a shifty scorer who can shoot the lights out, and he showed off his full toolkit against the Eagles. He’s rocketing up draft boards for his all-around ability. Illinois guard Quentin Coleman puts up the most points by a freshman this season against Winthrop: 35 PTS | 12-18 FG | 7 REB | 6 AST | 4 STL | 29 MIN pic.twitter.com/vUztGhpcrB — B/R Hoops (@brhoops) November 24, 2026 3. What was your favorite game you watched this week? Adam: Northwestern 79, Dayton 55 Northwestern won a basketball game, and that’s something I’m grateful for! But all jokes aside, it was fun seeing the ‘Cats play good basketball and it gave me hope that they will be able to win a few games in Big Ten play. The key for head coach Chris Collins is figuring out how to not get dominated in the paint despite being without Ryan Soulis and Luke McEldon (who the team recently announced will not be returning for the remainder of the season). On Sunday, it seemed like freshman center Symon Ghai offered a few answers, turning in impactful minutes during NU’s 29-4 first-half run. With Ghai impressing, my hopes for this team in Big Ten play have gone up from 0-1 wins to 3-4! Donovan: Villanova 79, Michigan 73 The Wolverines simply don’t have “it,“ and that became clear on Saturday. Senior guard Elliot Cadeau is a shadow of himself without three first-round draft picks in the starting lineup, and sophomore guard Trey McKenney is often more interested in goading the referees to call a flagrant due to his questionable actions than he is in actually trying to win games in crunch time. Villanova, a team that’s lost to Notre Dame and been destroyed by Pittsburgh, went up by 17 points against Michigan with about 10 minutes left, and then held on to beat the defending champs. The Wolverines tried to mount a late comeback, but they don’t have any truly frightening threats on the offensive end, and right now, they look like a group struggling through an identity crisis. The roster is loaded with talent, and Michigan will turn things around to some degree, but it won’t be competing for anything close to another National Championship. 4. What was your highlight reel of the week? Adam: Illinois sets Big Ten single-game record for three-pointers From top to bottom, the Big Ten shot the lights out this past week. On Friday, Purdue drained 21 threes against Oakland, tying the most made in a game in Big Ten history. HOURS LATER that same evening, Illinois one-upped the Boilermakers, pouring in 23 threes against Eastern Illinois en route to a 62-point victory in Champaign. The Illini shot 23-for-46 from the floor and had eight different players make shots from beyond the arc, including first-years Ethan Brown and Zavier Zens, who finished the night a combined 12-for-20 from deep, Tomislav Ivisic, who was 3-for-3, and Providence transfer Stefan Vaaks, who was 4-for-8. THE ILLINI MAKE B1G HISTORY 🤯 @IlliniMBB sets a new Big Ten single-game record with 23 three-pointers 👌 pic.twitter.com/cBS0wFvQQP — Big Ten Men's Basketball (@B1GMBBall) November 21, 2026 Donovan: Jaylen Crocker-Johnson’s 8-for-8 three-point shooting day Adding to my Minnesota praise from earlier, Jaylen Crocker-Johnson had himself a historic day in the Golden Gophers’ win over Utah. Crocker-Johnson scored a career-high 31 points, knocking down eight threes on eight attempts. That, my friends, is what you call perfection. The senior shot 32.3% from three-point range last season but is up to 51.2% on just under six attempts per game this year. Oh, and Crocker-Johnson just tied a program record for the most made threes in a single game. 8-8 🎯 🐊 Jaylen Crocker-Johnson career high points (31) and ties a program record for threes in the single game (8). #TeamTogether pic.twitter.com/CfMXpPdajK — Minnesota Men's Basketball (@GopherMBB) November 23, 2026 Judging overreactions 5. Minnesota will be a top-eight seed in the NCAA Tournament. Adam: NOT AN OVERREACTION The Golden Gophers have four players ranked in the Big Ten’s top 50 in EvanMiya.com’s Bayesian player rating — Isaac Asuma (11), Bobby Durkin (29), Grayson Grove (41) and Jaylen Crocker-Johnson (49). They are No. 19 on KenPom.com and one of 14 teams in the nation to be ranked top 30 in both the site’s offensive and defensive efficiency metrics. In other words, Minnesota’s got some hoopers AND they’re playing on a super high level as a team at the same time. And… the Golden Gophers are still hoping to add forward Cade Tyson, who averaged 19.6 points per game last year, to the mix, pending a ruling from a judge in Indiana. With what I’ve seen from them so far this year, I have no doubt the Gophers will finish the season as one of the Big Ten’s higher-seeded tournament teams. Donovan: NOT AN OVERREACTION I can’t jump off the bandwagon now. The Golden Gophers have three non-conference wins over high-major teams and have two more winnable opportunities against California and SMU over the next couple of weeks. Minnesota’s first two Big Ten games are about as hard as you can get, at Michigan State and against Illinois, but if it can go undefeated in the non-conference portion of its schedule and battle to a .500 record in Big Ten play, it should end up with a high seed in March. Asuma, Kyan Evans, Durkin and Crocker-Johnson have inspired Minnesota’s flying start, and the Golden Gophers might still be adding their best player from last season pending a court case decision. 6. Greg Gard is nearing the end of the road at Wisconsin. Adam: NOT AN OVERREACTION Gard led the Badgers to the Sweet 16 during his first two seasons as Wisconsin’s head coach. Since then, Wisconsin has had seven seasons with 20 or more wins but hasn’t made it to the second weekend of the NCAA Tournament ONCE. In two of the past three seasons, Gard’s Badgers have been upset in the first round, falling to James Madison in 2024 and High Point last year. For a program that has been as good as Wisconsin has been, those postseason results are unacceptable. Now, following the High Point loss, Gard suffered the worst mid-major loss (by far) of his tenure at Wisconsin six games into this season, falling 70-53 to Murray State. Wisco was run off the floor by the Racers, who currently rank No. 70 on KenPom.com. If the Badgers keep playing like this, they are going to have a tough time in the Big Ten, and it will be a battle for them to make the NCAA Tournament. So, in my eyes, Gard’s tenure in Madison is definitely becoming unstable. I’m not sure if he’s “nearing the end of the road,” but his seat is certainly starting to heat up. Donovan: OVERREACTION Gard is a great regular-season coach: Wisconsin has been a top-five seed in the NCAA Tournament in each of the past three years. Gard is not a great postseason coach: Wisconsin has not made it to the second weekend in each of the past three years. The Badgers’ early-season struggles aren’t overly concerning to me. Based on his history, I trust that Gard will turn things around and get his team into March Madness as a single-digit seed. Losses to Seton Hall and Murray State will not be the reason he is fired. However, I do have doubts about Gard’s ability to coach in the games that really matter. Another early flameout might be the end of his coaching career at Wisconsin, but I’m not going to bet on that just yet. 7. Michigan won’t be the same without Dusty May. Adam: OVERREACTION The Wolverines are struggling right now — there’s no doubt about that. However, keep in mind that it wasn’t just May who left the program in the offseason. Last year’s championship roster included THREE NBA lottery picks… and those players are all gone now! So this year, Michigan has taken a step back but it’s understandable. It had a major outflow of talent during the offseason, and it might take a couple years for it to stumble upon another championship-caliber roster. At the end of the day, it’s Michigan we’re talking about, the biggest basketball brand in the Big Ten. Things will be alright in Ann Arbor. Donovan: NOT AN OVERREACTION I don’t even think this is just about May’s absence; the entire Michigan athletic department is in shambles right now. It’s hard to operate as a successful basketball program when your school is in the headlines every day for another boneheaded decision. Michigan is a big brand and will always be relevant in national circles, but it must be remembered that it is a football-first school. When the basketball team is good, fans will come; when the team is mediocre to bad, fans will flood to the exits. Mike Boynton Jr. is not the guy to put butts in seats, and the program is headed for a lull like that of the Juwan Howard era. The bigger picture 8. Indiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, UCLA and USC are all undefeated so far. Looking at their schedules, which team do you think will stay that way the longest? Adam: Indiana It’s not ridiculous to say that No. 23 Indiana might not lose a basketball game for two more months. The Hoosiers play Bowling Green on Friday, Rutgers on Tuesday and Western Illinois next Thursday — those are all wins. Then it plays Iowa on the road — that will be a tough game, but Indiana has been the better team so far this season. Then Indiana hosts UCF, Missouri, FDU and No. 18 USC. USC will be a tight matchup, but with the Hoosiers at home in Assembly Hall, I think they pull it out. Then it plays Oregon, Washington, Maryland and Michigan — Darian DeVries’ squad is better than all of those teams this year. Indiana doesn’t play a game I think it will lose until it travels to The Barn on Jan. 20 to play Minnesota, when, presumably, it will be 19-0. Meanwhile, I think Minnesota will lose to No. 11 Michigan State or No. 4 Illinois over the next two weeks, USC will lose to No. 5 Texas Tech on Dec. 13 and Nebraska will lose at Creighton on Dec. 5. That leaves UCLA, which also should carry its winning streak into January. However, I think UCLA will fall either at Maryland or at home against the Spartans, ending its unbeaten run just before Indiana suffers its first loss a little further down the road. Donovan: Nebraska I might actually have the least confidence in Nebraska’s long-term potential out of this group of five undefeated Big Ten teams, but its schedule is just so easy. The Cornhuskers open conference play with Ohio State and Penn State, two teams that look incredibly beatable. Their toughest non-conference games are against a Missouri team that lost to Saint Louis and a Creighton team that barely beat Iowa and lost to Kansas State (Creighton’s win over Michigan doesn’t count for much; the Wolverines are going through something right now). Nebraska is an experienced team built to win early, and I think it will win those 50-50 games and reach 2027 at 14-0 before hosting Michigan State. Indiana will lose at Iowa, Minnesota will lose at Michigan State, UCLA will lose to Texas and USC will lose to Texas Tech. 9. Eleven Big Ten teams have already suffered multiple non-conference losses. Is the Big Ten in trouble? Adam: It’s concerning, but we’re alright The conference definitely doesn’t feel as deep as in years past, especially after this last week. Big Ten teams lost 12 non-conference games over the past week, and the league has only seven teams ranked in KenPom.com’s top 40. Last year, it had nine in the top 30. But the top of the conference still sports some of the nation’s best teams, with Illinois, Michigan State and UCLA currently all legitimate national title contenders. The Big Ten will still have teams making deep tournament runs this year, and I think Underwood’s Illini are going to win it all. So, things are going to be OK. Donovan: YES!!! There are only seven teams in the conference that I feel confident in right now. Only two of those teams have flashed championship-winning quality. The middle and bottom of the Big Ten are getting eaten alive, which will only come back to hurt the teams at the top when they drop unexpected games. The Big Ten doesn’t have quantity or quality so far, and it desperately needs teams like Ohio State, Michigan and Purdue to start stringing together some wins. Looking ahead 10. What are you excited about next week? Adam: Wisconsin vs. Northwestern on Tuesday How good or bad are the ‘Cats? We’re going to find out in a big way Tuesday night when Northwestern plays its first Big Ten opponent, hosting the Badgers at Welsh-Ryan Arena. While I wouldn’t necessarily say I’m excited for this game, I’m definitely anxious to see the result. Donovan: The start of Big Ten play!!! On Tuesday night, it all begins. Believe it or not, Big Ten play is right around the corner. Iowa and Purdue kick things off, followed by three more big-time matchups. All 18 teams will play two conference games in early December, giving fans a taste of what’s to come. I’m especially looking forward to Minnesota’s trip to East Lansing on Wednesday.

title: Thanksgiving reunion: Rick Pitino meets Louisville for first time since exit
summary: St. John's vs. Louisville will be the first time Rick Pitino faces the program he won a national championship with, but had a tumultuous exit with.
content: LAS VEGAS – Thanksgiving is going to be an emotional one for Rick Pitino . The St. John's coach will see a familiar face on Thursday, Nov. 26: Louisville , as he's facing the Cardinals in the Players Era 16 semifinals for the first time since his exit from the program in 2017. When it was confirmed the Red Storm would play his old team, Pitino said he didn't have any thoughts, more focused on the fact his team didn't close out the 90-79 win over Oregon in the first round of the tournament. But make no mistake, this will be a game that certainly impacts the coach. "There's a lot of emotion that goes into that," ESPN analyst Jay Bilas told reporters. Pitino spent 16 seasons at Louisville, winning 293 games and the 2013 national championship, its first since 1986. However, scandal was what led to his demise. Pitino was fired in October 2017 after the program was part of an FBI investigation into corruption within college basketball recruiting, which came after a sex scandal in which escorts were paid to dance for and have sex with players and recruits. That also led to Louisville vacating 123 wins, the 2013 national championship and its 2012 Final Four appearance. Despite the tumultuous exit and nearly a decade since then, Pitino is still revered in Louisville, and it holds a place in his heart. He plans to be at Louisville's KFC Yum! Center on Jan. 2 when the program will honor longtime Louisville sports information director Kenny Klein, who died in June at age 66, with a banner-raising ceremony. Klein also joined Pitino at St. John's as a special advisor for the 2024-25 season. Louisville coach Pat Kelsey said, "it would be absolutely electric" to see Pitino return to his former home. "A big part of Louisville is Rick Pitino," said coach Pat Kelsey. "In my opinion, he's one of the legendary coaches in the history of the game. He's on the Mount Rushmore." More: Rick Pitino questions expanded March Madness pushback: 'Why and who cares?' Since bringing St. John's from its slumber to a Big East contender, it always felt like it was a matter of when − not if − Pitino would tangle with his old program. It unfortunately won't be taking place at Madison Square Garden or in Louisville, but rather at Michelob Ultra Arena in Las Vegas, which won't have anywhere near the full crowd a game of this magnitude calls for. But for the Louisville fans that made the holiday trip, they'll likely give a warm reception to their old coach. While he didn't offer any emotions or thoughts, Pitino did give the Cardinals credit for being a quality team coming off a big win against Texas Tech. "They've been playing well most of the season. They had a bad half against Memphis, but we had a bad 10 minutes. That happens, but they're very talented. We know we're going to have to play a lot better to beat a team like that. So we'll see what happens," he said. You also can't forget about the ramifications of the game. The winner will move to the Players Era 16 Michelob Ultra championship round, with the shot at winning the whole tournament in the final on Saturday, Nov. 28. It's the reunion that makes it all that more enticing, creating a Thanksgiving matchup that will have the college basketball world locked in. "It's going to be fun," Bilas said. "It won't be fun for Pat or Rick, but it'll be fun for everybody else." This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Thanksgiving reunion: Rick Pitino meets Louisville for first time since exit

title: Todd Golden calls out Florida's performance in win over Milwaukee
summary: After Florida basketball's win over Milwaukee, Todd Golden discusses what went wrong in the narrow home victory.
content: A nine-point victory over Milwaukee wasn’t enough to satisfy Florida basketball head coach Todd Golden, who expressed frustration with his team’s defensive effort and bench production following Tuesday night’s 76-67 win. The Gators entered the contest as favorites by more than 30 points. Still, instead of cruising to a comfortable victory, Florida found itself in a surprisingly competitive matchup against a Milwaukee squad that refused to go away. Although the Orange and Blue eventually created enough separation down the stretch to secure the win, their performance left plenty to be desired in the eyes of their head coach. Here's a full breakdown of Golden's remarks following the Gators' victory over Milwaukee. Todd Golden's opening statement First of all, credit to Milwaukee. I thought they did a really good job of kind of dictating the terms of the game. We couldn't get any pace in the game tonight. I think it was only about 60 possessions. They want to kind of slow it down and grind it out. We were unable to flip it that way. And then they beat the scout a little bit. Their bigs, I think, had combined to make one or two 3s all year and hit five tonight. I think that allowed to gain a little bit of confidence and stick around a little bit. They did a good job. I thought they had a good game plan. We were unable to really flip it. We obviously got to play a little bit better next week with Duke coming in. But at the end of the day, we'll take this win and trying to get our juice and mojo back going into the Duke game next week. How much of a surprise was the defensive effort considering how much emphasis you put on being a defensive team? It's going to be a tough one to evaluate because we held them to 16-for-40 from two. We held them to 40% from two, which is really good. We kept them off the line. They only got six free throws. We obviously didn't turn them over at all, but the game was all about the 3-point line for them. They made 10 3s out of 19 attempts. Our game plan was to contain penetration and we're going to live with their non-shooting front court taking 3s. Well they made five. There was one point — I think they had 39 points or 43 points and 12 of those were off their 3s. So I'm like, this was in the second half; it's a tricky one because we are obviously not ok with allowing 52% from behind the line. Collectively, as a team, they shot 44% from the field. I think our two-point field-goal defense was a lot better. We did a good job of making them miss. Our 3-point line defense was not quite good enough. I don't have as much of a problem with their front court guys like, Amadou went 3-for-3 from the 3-point line. I don't think he had made a three coming into the game. Malosa had made a couple. He was 1-for-2. Jovanovich had not made a 3 on the season. He made one. So that was a little of a rug-pull for us on the defensive end. I'm more happy with our 2-point field goal defense. The 3-point defense with Jackson at the end was not good enough, knowing that the only way he could really stay in the game late was giving him opportunities to knock them down. I don't think our communication was good enough defensively; I don't think our sense of urgency was good enough. A little better around the rim, but collectively not good enough. What does Alex Lloyd need to do defensively to get more minutes? Play with energy and toughness on the defensive end and dictate. How satisfying was Rueben's performance, especially with no fouls? As we've talked about, he has received a lot of criticism to start the year for not producing at the level we all know he is capable of. But we as a staff felt pretty confident that getting him back here, getting back comfortable and letting it go a little bit, then it'd be just okay. He delivered for us tonight. I thought he was fantastic. It's one of his best games since he's been here. He settled us on the offensive end. He did a great job finishing, made his free throws, created a lot of second-chance opportunities for us and cleaned up on the defensive glass. He played like a Preseason All-American, like a first-team all-leaguer tonight. On Rueben Chinyelu making a 3 Time and score, man. You know, I didn't love it to be honest. But, at the same time — and I heard these guys talking about it — he does put in a lot of time. He's a guy that — he's obviously very prideful and has a lot of belief. And, with the work that he puts in, you got to live with one of your best players letting it fly every now and again. On the different combinations, bench Yeah, I thought our bench was bad tonight, to be honest. You know, I thought Jones actually played really well. He was plus-12 in seven minutes. He guarded, was good on the defensive glass. Got a nice dunk, three blocks. He gave us a lift. I thought AJ Brown actually gave us good minutes. I thought he was tough. I thought he was physical, played with good purpose. But I thought Alex, Domen and Isaiah weren't good enough. And, I think that's going to be a little bit of a swing for us. I think all three of those guys are very capable. Our staff has a high level of belief in them. But, when you come in the game, the expectation is that the level is at least staying the same, if not, going up in terms of the energy, and we didn't get that from them tonight. Was there a casualness from the team tonight? Again, I think we're dealing with a couple of different things in this game. We're coming off Vegas where we played three games in three days. We're still a little fatigued. That's just the reality of it. We played our main guys a lot of minutes out there, and I felt like our first group was not up to par in terms of their communication defensively. I thought their effort was fine, but their communication led to some easy breakdowns and baskets. And, I did not think our bench played with enough fire. I don't know how else to say it. I didn't think they were flying around. When they came in the game, they were getting scored on. If you take Jones out of the equation, our bench was minus-19. So, I think that says all that you need to know. On what he said to the guys in the locker room, addressing frustrations with the game We addressed it. This is something that we're not tiptoeing around it. One of the great things about where our program is, our guys, we talk about it a lot, for lack of a better term, the standard of what we expect. We're going to be ok if guys make mistakes, if they're playing with their hair on fire and they're flying around. We're not going to be ok if we don't feel like we are. I told the guys what we were disappointed with tonight, whether it was myself, Carlin, Korey, other coaches; we felt like we were coaching effort a little bit tonight. And, that's just not something that we're going to do. So, moving forward, I think it's pretty clear what the expectation is from those guys when they get the opportunity. And, again, it's not that they can't mess up. Everybody messes up. I mess up. Our best players mess up, but you got to play with a level of effort and exertion that is noticeable. And I did not think that we did that tonight. Was this the most intense postgame locker room speech for you since the early years? I don't know if it was intense as much as just very honest. Very black and white in terms of what we felt like we saw in our performance. And, again, we won by 9. It could have been a lot worse. That's a game that if we are even a little more off our game, they come in here and win. So, it's not the end of the world, but we want to nip this thing and make sure that we get those things in order. Especially for a really, really, really talented Duke team that comes in here next week. title: Choosing Between Manzardo and Ingle
summary: Looking at left-handed hitting options
content: CLEVELAND, OHIO - JUNE 27: Kyle Manzardo #9 and Kahlil Watson #31 of the Cleveland Guardians celebrate scoring on a single hit by Cooper Ingle for Ingle's first Major League base hit during the fourth inning against the Seattle Mariners at Progressive Field on June 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Guardians may be looking to put Cooper Ingle or Kyle Manzardo on their 2027 team as a left-handed hitter. Which player is the better choice? Last season was pretty much a disaster for Kyle Manzardo. After putting up a 112 wRC+ and 27 homers in 2025, one could have been reasonably optimistic the 26 year-old would make a moderate step forward and provide a needed threat in the Guardians’ lineup with the 120 wRC+ he was projected for by several systems. Instead, Manzardo managed only a 94 wRC+ before getting demoted to Columbus for the last two months of the year. Really, the only positive for Manzardo is that he had +3 Defensive Runs Saved at first base compared with -5 there in 2025. Unfortunately, Manzardo’s Outs Above Average and Fielding Run Values were still well underwater so the jury is certainly still out on his value as a defender. Manzardo went down and put up a 114 wRC+ in Columbus, and still had only a .307 xwOBA, part of why he didn’t get another chance to impact the team in September or October, I am sure. It’s a little hard to understand why Manzardo took such a step back. His chase rate, contact rates and hard-hit rates declined by a few percentage points, which isn’t ideal, but nothing alarming. Somehow, however, it amounted to a .060 decline in ISO, which is significant and not something Manzardo can sustain and be a decent major league player. He needs to be in the .225-.250 ISO area. So, the question is… can he get back to that? In an odd way, Manzardo is a sort of reverse Jo Adell. Adell has his issues with contact, but, for his career, he is best in situations where it matters most. Adell has a 117 wRC+ with runners in scoring position. Meanwhile, Manzardo has an 84 wRC+ with RISP. Both have defensive issues and big platoon splits (Adell 81/125 RHP/LHP, Manzardo 108/82 RHP/LHP). But, Adell is typically getting it done when his team needs RBIs. Are these numbers predictive? MLB history would tell us they are probably not sticky; generally speaking, if you are given enough opportunities, your overall numbers for hitting will match with your numbers with RISP. But, the question remains whether or not Manzardo is swinging too early and too wildly with runners in scoring position and if that’s an approach that can be adjusted. Meanwhile, Cooper Ingle is projected by Steamer and FGDC for a 106 wRC+, which can probably be expected to be higher if Ingle receives reps mostly against RHP as he has prominent splits over the past two seasons with an OPS over .900 vs RHP and around .600 vs LHP. Ingle had a 151 wRC+ in the minors last year and a .297/.424/.597 slashline. Now, this was partially fueled by a .362 BABIP (and a .989 OPS in the friendly confines of Columbus as compared to an .862 OPS on the road) but his xwOBA of .362 is still a good number (while significantly lower than his wOBA of .421). He had a 23/18 K/BB% which was a significant jump in strikeouts from his previous minor league average of around 15% K%, but seemed to reflect a desire to get more power… an approach that worked spectacularly, seeing his ISO go from .159 to .231 and his average exit velocity rising by 2 mph while increasing his launch angle by 7 degrees. Ingle got a seven-game trial period in Cleveland that was terrible as he had a -6 wRC+ and made a couple crucial errors in left field. I don’t think it’s wise to read much of anything into the hitting failure, but it’s an open question whether he will be able to field in left or at catcher at the major league level. At that point, the question would become if this 5’8 frame can reasonably be expected to be a competent platoon-DH because he is too short to play first base. Probably not, so Ingle needs to spend the offseason making sure he can be relied on as at least a third archer and a part-time outfielder. If so, I think it’s reasonable for the Guardians to believe he can provide a 110 wRC+ or better vs. RHP as a pairing for Angel Martinez in left and Jo Adell at DH, while spelling Bailey once a week behind the dish. In looking at both players, there isn’t a clear answer but Manzardo and Ingle are at least intriguing options. I would like to see if the Guardians can add another left-handed bat who can play corner outfield (Larnach, Wallner, Raley, or a trade target) and/or first base in free agency to bring depth to this role, but, if not, I do think it’s rational to give Manzardo and Ingle first chance to win that roster spot and look to upgrade mid-season as needed. Of course, all of that depends on there being a season at all! Let me know what you think about Manzardo and Ingle for 2027 in the comments below.

title: Detroit Tigers Sign Two Familiar Faces
summary: Scott Harris and the Detroit Tigers have brought back two familiar faces after non-tendering them last week.
content: The Detroit Tigers are bringing back a pair of familiar faces just one week after parting ways with them. According to Tigers beat writer Evan Woodbery of MLive, the organization has signed infielder Trey Sweeney and left-handed pitcher Jake Miller to minor-league contracts after non-tendering both players last week. The moves allow Tigers president of baseball operations Scott Harris to retain both players without committing spots on the 40-man roster. It is a strategy that has become somewhat familiar during Harris’ tenure in Detroit. Sep 23, 2025; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; Detroit Tigers shortstop Trey Sweeney (27) throws to first in the third inning against the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field. Mandatory Credit: David Richard-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters) Detroit Tigers Re-Sign Trey Sweeney and Jake Miller Both signings are confirmed on the Tigers’ official transaction page , which lists the moves as taking place on November 25. Sweeney and Miller had been among the four players Detroit designated for assignment on November 17 before officially becoming free agents. Sweeney, 26, provides the Tigers with additional infield depth as he works to reestablish himself following an injury-plagued 2026 campaign. Although there is no guarantee he will return to the major league roster, keeping him in the organization makes sense for Detroit. Meanwhile, Miller, 25, is an intriguing left-handed pitching prospect who missed a significant portion of last season with a hip injury. According to NBC Sports , Miller posted a 0.77 ERA and struck out 24 batters across 23 1/3 minor-league innings in 2026. Scott Harris Continues Familiar Roster-Building Strategy As Woodbery pointed out Thursday morning, Harris has had considerable success convincing players who have been non-tendered to return to the Tigers on minor-league contracts. The strategy allows Detroit to retain organizational depth while maintaining flexibility on its 40-man roster. Sweeney and Miller were two of the three players the Tigers non-tendered ahead of last week’s deadline , with outfielder Matt Vierling being the other. Whether Vierling could eventually return to the organization remains to be seen. Neither signing is going to generate the excitement of a major free-agent acquisition, but these are the types of low-risk moves that can pay dividends over the course of a 162-game season. In Miller’s case, particularly, there is enough upside to make bringing him back a worthwhile investment.

title: Former Arizona pitcher Kevin Ginkel signs with Twins
summary: Assuming there’s a Major League Baseball season in 2027, which is a big if, Kevin Ginkel will be playing it for a different team than the one with which he’s spent the first decade of his professional career. The former Arizona pitcher has reportedly signed a 2-year deal with the Minnesota Twins. The contract is […]
content: Kevin Ginkel during the eighth inning of NLCS Game 7. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Assuming there’s a Major League Baseball season in 2027, which is a big if, Kevin Ginkel will be playing it for a different team than the one with which he’s spent the first decade of his professional career. The former Arizona pitcher has reportedly signed a 2-year deal with the Minnesota Twins. The contract is expected to be worth $18 million, per Jeff Passan of ESPN . The 32-year-old Ginkel finally reached free agency after eight seasons with the Arizona Diamondbacks, the team that drafted him in the 22nd round in 2016. He appeared in 341 MLB games from 2019-26, 3rd-most in franchise history, serving as both a closer and setup man in the bullpen. Ginkel was 6-4 with three saves and a 4.12 ERA in a career-high 74 games in 2026, striking out 72 in 67.2 innings. Since making his MLB debut he’s won 28 games and saved 19 during the regular season, and in the DBacks’ run to the World Series in 2023 he tossed 11.2 scoreless innings over 10 playoff outings. A member of the UA’s College World Series team in 2016, Ginkel spent just one season with the Wildcats after transferring from Southwest College. During the 2016 season he was 5-1 with a 2.80 ERA in 25 games with seven starts. The Twins finished 77-85 last season but have been aggressive in free agency this month. In addition to Ginkel they signed starter Sonny Gray and re-signed catcher Ryan Jeffers .

title: Free agent catcher returns to Mets ahead of deadline
summary: The 29-year-old gives the Mets a valuable defender behind the plate
content: On Tuesday, Dec. 1, teams across MLB face a deadline that is growing harder by the day. If the league locks out players as expected, it will result in a freeze on transactions involving 40-man roster players that might not end until a new Collective Bargaining Agreement between players and owners is ratified. The free agent frenzy that kicked off with Tarik Skubal agreeing to terms with the New York Mets on Sunday is a direct result of the deadline. Hayden Senger could have waited until after Dec. 1 to sign a minor league contract, but the Mets didn’t want to wait to bring the catcher back. MORE: Mets lose 29-year-old infielder to Dodgers in free agency According to his official transactions log, Senger and the Mets agreed to a minor league contract Thursday. The 29-year-old backstop has spent his entire MLB career with the New York Mets. In 40 games over the last two seasons, Senger is hitting .172 (15 for 87) with one home run and six RBIs. His ability with a bat makes him the Mets’ clear number-3 catcher behind Francisco Alvarez and Luis Torrens. Defensively, Senger is an above-average pitch framer and blocker , and thrower on stolen-base attempts according to Statcast. MORE: Mets, Tarik Skubal agree to record-shattering $450 million contract A 24th-round draft pick out of Miami (Ohio) University in 2018, Senger persevered for six years in the minor leagues before making his big league debut. He has played 524 affiliated minor league games and 13 in the Dominican Winter League, compared to just 40 in the majors. Remarkably, Senger has stayed with the Mets organization that whole time. That won’t change in 2027, even though he was eligible to sign anywhere — and anytime — as a free agent this winter. — Enjoy free coverage of the top news & trending stories with The Big Lead Newsletter —

title: For Goldschmidt, There Was Nothing the Mets ‘Needed To Sell Me On’
summary: When the New York Mets reached out to Paul Goldschmidt — who officially signed with the club on Wednesday to a one-year, $8 million deal — he was excited. He knew manager Andy Green already and believes it's a talented squad that has World Series aspirations. "I'm excited to be part of the Mets," Goldschmidt …
content: Sep 18, 2026; Phoenix, Arizona, USA; New York Yankees infielder Paul Goldschmidt (48) watches on from the dugout in the sixth inning of a game against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field. Mandatory Credit: Allan Henry-Imagn Images | Source: Lastwordonsports.com - Augustus Oswald, Site Editor When the New York Mets reached out to Paul Goldschmidt — who officially signed with the club on Wednesday to a one-year, $8 million deal — he was excited. He knew manager Andy Green already and believes it’s a talented squad that has World Series aspirations. “I’m excited to be part of the Mets,” Goldschmidt said. “They have a really great team, a lot of really great players. [I saw it] last year with some of the new younger players that either made their debut or had their full first season, as well as mixed in with some of the trades and some of the guys that have been here. … The expectations of this organization are to win the World Series from the outside looking in, and I have no doubt that the players, coaches, front office and ownership feel the same way. So it’s exciting, and I’m ready to go.” First baseman Paul Goldschmidt and the New York Yankees are finalizing a one-year contract, sources tell ESPN. Goldschmidt, 38, returns to the Yankees after hitting .274/.328/.403 for them last season. — Jeff Passan (@JeffPassan) February 6, 2026 For Goldschmidt, There Was Nothing the Mets ‘Needed To Sell Me On’ Goldschmidt’s role with the Mets is not something that would be new for him. Over the last year and a half, the 39-year-old spent time platooning with New York Yankees first baseman Ben Rice since the second half of 2025. Before that, Goldschmidt was an everyday starter. The seven-time All-Star is expected to platoon at first base, sharing the position with Jared Young. Goldschmidt will get most of his playing time facing left-handed pitching while Young will take on the righties. But for Goldschmidt, joining the Mets wasn’t about how much playing time he would get, but rather it was about the team being “the right fit.” “My concern was not ‘hey, how do I go to some place where I get the most playing time.’ My concern was [about] going to a team where it felt right,” Goldschmidt said. “It’s hard to kind of put that into words. Just to have an opportunity to be on a team that has a chance to win and is going for, obviously the Mets are in that. [In my role] I said I’m ready to do whatever [I can]. I’m going to prepare to be ready to play every day if you need me to, but whatever decision is best for the team, whatever you need me to do, I’m open to doing it, and I’m gonna do it to the best of my ability.” Sep 24, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt (48) hits an RBI single against the Tampa Bay Rays during the seventh inning at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images This season, Goldschmidt’s numbers against left-handers were among some of the best. Goldschmidt had a strong age-38 season with the Yankees, showing age isn’t slowing him down. He slashed .252/.313/.452 with 18 home runs, 52 RBIs and a .765 OPS across 105 games. Goldschmidt is a known lefty killer, and the veteran produced tremendous numbers against southpaws this year. In 183 plate appearances, he posted a .299 batting average, 11 home runs, a .967 OPS, and a WRC+ of 168. It didn’t take the Mets much convincing to get Goldschmidt to come from the Bronx to the Queens. Owner Steve Cohen’s devotion to winning, as Goldschmidt remembers hearing about it from past years, was what helped attract him to the Mets. “I remember hearing it a few years ago when guys like [Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander] came here,” Goldschmidt said. … Just how bad [Cohen] wants to win, how bad this whole organization is committed to winning. So I think I knew that going in, and you’ve seen obviously there’s been some ups and downs as far as the team’s performance over the last few years, but you’ve seen [in 2024] how close they were to getting to and potentially winning the World Series. Honestly, being with the other team in New York, you know the expectations of this city and seeing it firsthand that there was nothing that anyone really needed to sell me on.” Sep 12, 2026; Bronx, New York, USA; New York Yankees first baseman Paul Goldschmidt (48) hits a double in the fourth inning against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Wendell Cruz-Imagn Images Goldschmidt said he’s had good conversations with Green back in Arizona when he was still in the minor leagues. That connection can and certainly will carry over as the entire team gets together prior to the start of the season. Along with Goldschmidt’s role of platooning at first, being a leader and mentor is something that he’ll be expected to do. It comes naturally with the age, but even more so with the level of success that he’s had. The Last Word Guys like A.J. Ewing, Carson Benge, and other young players like Juan Soto, for that matter too, will surely be picking the decorated brain of Goldschmidt, who recalled some of the players whose brains he picked when he arrived in MLB. Now, he feels like it’s time to give back. “I had so many great role models. When I got to the big leagues, guys like Xavier Nady , Willie Bloomquist , JJ Putz , the list goes on and on. I probably don’t have time to list them all, and I hope those guys know how much they’ve impacted my career. … The experience I’ve had — the ups and downs, the good and the bad — you can kind of share to hopefully help [the younger guys] perform. I think seeing these younger players with the Mets that have come up the last few years is exciting, and hopefully I can help them in a small way.” Main Photo Credit: Allan Henry-Imagn Images More New York Mets News: Why the Mets Should Take a Chance on 31-Year-Old FA Pitcher What A.J. Ewing’s Extension Reveals About the Mets How the Mets Landed Tarik Skubal

title: Holidays on OTM: What are you thankful for this Thanksgiving?
summary: I’m thankful that a guy like Payton Tolle figures to be a part of this situation for a while. It’s been far too long since we’ve had a legit capital-P Personality in the organization—someone who is, to borrow a phrase from your old report cards in school, a pleasure to have in class. Red Sox […]
content: Thanksgiving or Halloween dinner with baked chicken with potatoes and lemons on big ceramic dish, pumpkin pies, yellow autumn leaves and pumpkins as decorations over linen table cloth. Rustic style. (Photo by: Natasha Breen/REDA/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) I’m thankful that a guy like Payton Tolle figures to be a part of this situation for a while. It’s been far too long since we’ve had a legit capital-P Personality in the organization—someone who is, to borrow a phrase from your old report cards in school, a pleasure to have in class. Red Sox Nation deserves a guy like Tolle to root for. It doesn’t hurt that he’s filthy on the mound, too. — Fitzy Mo Peña I’m thankful for the Summer 2026 Red Sox. I know the opinion on the site is that this season was a tremendous failure because of the “playoff” “series” in New York and I will continue to strongly disagree. The 15-game winning streak was some of the most fun baseball the team has played since 2004. The planes not cooperating, flying cross country, playing series after series in the streak on the road? All the different time zones and game starts. It was electric. — Mike Carlucci Say what you will about the way Chad Tracy managed the bullpen in the Yankees series in particular, but he hadn’t been there before and it didn’t look like it was shaping up to be the Red Sox’s year, anyway. On a team that has started to embrace developing younger talent over fighting in free agency to get established names (unless said name comes with some volatility and a smaller price tag) it’s good that the manager not only has experience managing some of the centerpieces on this roster, such as Roman Anthony, but also doesn’t shy away from doing so, like a certain other manager . With these players, some in their ugly duckling stage and still others being cast members from the Island of Misfit Toys (wrong holiday, I know) it’s important to have a manager who knows that development doesn’t happen in a vacuum. It’s important to have a manager who uses the game to teach rather than simply saying “we just gotta play better.” Though the Yankees series still burns, Chad Tracy, new in his own role, oversees a team of players with a high ceiling, and I’m thankful he’s leading the ship into 2027. – Dean Roussel I’m thankful for Fenway Fridays. In 2025, I watched on my couch when Ceddanne “swing and a DRIIIIIIIVE” Rafaela walked it off against Tampa Bay, when Payton Tolle made his debut against the Pirates, and when Rafaela (again) walked it off to clinch a playoff spot in the final weekend against the Tigers. I told myself I’d be at Fenway more often in 2026 to see the Friday Greens, and I didn’t regret it one bit. There’s a whole different vibe in the park at 7:10 on those days, which goes beyond “it’s the weekend” excitement. The Red Sox may have been inconsistent from month to month this season, but they finished with a record of 13 and 2 at home on Fridays in 2026. Only 13 of those games were scheduled before the season, but rainouts that were rescheduled as Friday doubleheaders against the Rays in July and the Cubs in September both resulted in sweeps. Fenway Fridays will be included during Grace on Thursday. – Bob Osgood I’m thankful for OTM and the community here — Both my follow writers and all the commenters! As we approach a lockout, I’m grateful to know I’ve got a place to read and share ideas about the sport and team we all love. What’s coming next isn’t going to be easy, but this place and this group will help us all get through it. – Matthew Gross

title: What the LL staff is thankful for this year
summary: Looking back on what we’re thankful for in 2026, Seattle Mariners edition
content: Oct 1, 2023; Seattle, Washington, USA; Seattle Mariners center fielder Julio Rodriguez (44) eats cotton candy while walking around the warning track following a 1-0 victory against the Texas Rangers at T-Mobile Park. Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con Happy Thanksgiving! Many years, we publish a collaborative piece around Thanksgiving talking about what we’re grateful for in the Mariners season of the past year. Some years are a tougher lift than others, and 2026 is one of the toughest (ones tonight) in recent memory. Still, a baseball season is long, and even in this misery of a season, there are joyful moments to pull out to keep us warm over the long, dark off-season. As November draws to a close and the lockout looms, it feels even more important to set these things down so we can revisit them on days we’re staring out the window and feeling like the waiting might never end. Feel free to leave what you’re thankful for in the comments, and as always, we’re thankful for you, the readers, who make what we do possible – in the good years and the bad. Kate: Beauty in the Breakdown Not to sugarcoat it: living through the 2026 season was largely an exercise in misery, even allowing for the occasional fun moments. I’ve never looked forward to the end of homestands before, but caught myself counting down several times this season, metaphorically counting down days with little tally marks on the walls of the press box. It was embarrassing, to be the discussion point of so much discourse about “most disappointing team in baseball”, and an especially crushing blow after being the focal point of so much glowing praise last season. The 2026 Seattle Mariners embarrassed me, something I thought I’d long moved past. But to quote Denis Johnson in Jesus’ Son : “No more pretending for him! He was completely and openly a mess. Meanwhile the rest of us go on trying to fool each other.” The 2026 Mariners were completely and openly a mess, and that in its own way is beautiful in its utter lack of pretension. And because it was such a spectacular failure, it made the fixes equally sweeping in scope. I’m really excited by the infusion of youthful energy in the new coaching staff – specifically Tanner Swanson, who has been a dream coaching target of mine for years – and the recommitment to connecting the processes in the minor league side of the organization with the big-league club. Control the zone redux! I think there’s something brave and beautiful about being willing to say “I failed” with your whole chest and then aim to do better – to borrow again from Samuel Beckett: “Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better.” Eric: Thank you, Randy The only memory of the 2026 Mariners I will hold onto is that we got to see the elite version of Randy Arozarena. The “some mf named Randy” version who terrorized opponents in the 2020 postseason and bat flipped his way into the hearts of fans who enjoy players with personality. We saw flashes of it in 2024 and 2025, but he seemed to look around at the eternal struggle-bus lineup this team was rolling out in 2026 and said, “Fuck it, I’ll do it myself.” The left field defense and “gentleman’s doubles” are part of the charm. He turned it on when he needed to but otherwise I think he just saved all his energy for mashing at the plate and posted his best offensive season by a pretty good margin at 5.7 WAR and slashed .281/.381/.484, numbers that are honestly even more impressive than I was expecting them to be when I looked them up just now. The team may have been fried ass, but Randy balled out in ways we’ve only seen a handful of times from Mariners players. Thanks again, Randy. You’ll always be a favorite. View Link Isabelle: A Peaceful October This is the epitome of selfishness, but if ever there was a year for the Mariners to be non-competitive, I am so glad they were this year. John and I got engaged in July and, shortly after, decided that due to some family health issues it would be better to get married sooner rather than later. Baseball is no longer either of our primary jobs, but it does still occupy a good chunk of our time (and our people’s time) – particularly so during a playoff run. It wouldn’t have been a dealbreaker, but it definitely made things easier. With the support of friends and family, and with the Seattle Mariners refusal to play compelling baseball or capitalize on the weakest division in the league, we were able to plan a wedding in about two and a half months, with all our loved ones in attendance. It was stressful, chaotic and particularly emotional, but also replete with opportunities for silver linings like this along the way. Now, with all that said, here’s hoping many future wedding anniversary plans have to be rearranged to accommodate the Mariners’ playoff schedule. Nicky V: We’re So Back I sat out the entirety of the 2025 season, up until the ALCS, for a few different reasons that ended up sending me into an identity crisis and a self-imposed shame spiral about it all. So even though the 2026 season Sucked, super bad, I am thankful that I got to strap in for the ride. Watching Colt Emerson hit sub-.200 and 39 games of Brendan Donovan enriched my life in a way that is unique to awful Mariners baseball. Now, I look forward to being enriched by good Mariners baseball, something I’ve yet to truly experience. John: The Difference – Flume, Toro y Moi My favorite experience watching baseball in 2026 was seeing the World Baseball Classic unfold in San Juan, Puerto Rico and then Miami. My second-favorite came in the twilight hours of summer, joined with Isabelle and a few friends for our last chance to see the Mariners face the Athletics in Sacramento. It was a disastrous series for Seattle, sandwiching one of the season’s few joyful blowout victories with two crushing losses. Sunday’s defeat was one of many moments the season could be declared over, but watching Randy Arozarena, statuesque, processing for what felt like several minutes in left field as the rest of the stadium sortied is indelibly etched in my mind. And yet, the weekend was a delight. Three days of baseball in late summer sun, with an Arizona Fall League vibe of detachment. I heard Henry Bolte’s walkup song what felt assuredly to be upwards of 48 times, and despite its ominous portents it became too catchy to ignore. I will take it forward into the winter and beyond, and hope to hear it with joy under the light of future suns. Zach: Ryan Rowland-Smith, Croco-dinger Hunter In a season I’d rather forget, the image I’m sure I won’t is Ryan Rowland-Smith wrestling an inflatable alligator after improbably hitting a pair of home runs to pay off weeks of anticipation. Hyphen has always managed to make Pick-Me Energy more charming than it has any right to be, and his willingness to participate in the Alumni Home Run Derby funneled that in the most positive possible direction. The fact that he actually knocked not just one, but two out to right field—and listening to Goldy and Gary lose their damn minds—was a pinnacle of parasocialism. Goldy and Gary both give Hyphen an incredibly hard time, but it’s always obvious that it’s in a “he’s our goofball, don’t you dare say a mean word about him” way. For them to get this excited over an improbable achievement was stronger evidence of their love than anything I could imagine them saying to him directly. But what made it land is that I feel exactly the same way. Crikey, what a moment!

title: Mariners News: Alec Bohm, Kevin Gausman, and Foster Griffin
summary: Celebrating Turkey Day with a deluge of free agent signings around baseball.
content: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 30: Alec Bohm #28 of the Philadelphia Phillies runs the bases after hitting a home run against the Atlanta Braves during the tenth inning in game two of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park on September 30, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Edward M. Pio Roda/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning friends and happy Thanksgiving! Yesterday provided another whirlwind of signings with the free agency period closing on Tuesday night. Let’s get you all of the latest news as you begin your cooking prep. In Mariners news… Kate Preusser wonders if Maikel García can put his injury-plagued 2026 season behind him to thrive for the Mariners in 2027 and beyond. Will the Mariners make another move before the lockout begins on December 1? Join the conversation . Around the league… The Royals found García’s replacement, signing third baseman Alec Bohm to a two-year, $20M deal. The Padres signed left-hander JoJo Romero to a three-year, $21M contract. The Guardians are bringing back lefty Foster Griffin on a three-year, $48M pact. The 36-year-old right-hander Kevin Gausman landed with the Tigers on a one-year, $25M contract. The Brewers bolstered their bullpen with a one-year, $4.75M deal with righty Antonio Senzatela. Catcher Gary Sánchez is headed to the Marlins on a one-year, $6.5M deal. Luis Robert, Jr. is returning to the Orioles on a one-year, $12M contract. The Rockies inked deals with a pair of left-handed pitchers, agreeing to a two-year, $32M deal with David Peterson and a three-year, $42M contract with Patrick Sandoval . Righty reliever Kevin Ginkel is headed to the Twins on a two-year, $18M deal. The Nationals signed left-hander A.J. Puk to a one-year, $5M contract. Major League Baseball handed out its pre-arbitration bonus pool earnings . NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong took home the largest slice of the pie with $3.5M. The Yankees are hiring former Orioles manager Brandon Hyde to serve as bench coach. Major League Baseball is suing the MLBPA in order to have the lockout declared “legal” to forestall any effort by the players to challenge the work stoppage with antitrust legislation.

title: How the Mets’ plans at first base look after signing Paul Goldschmidt
summary: The Mets seem to be working towards a lefty-rightly platoon at first.
content: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 30: Jared Young #29 of the New York Mets gets set against the Houston Astros during the game at Citi Field on August 30, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Caean Couto/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Mets coming to terms with Paul Goldschmidt on a one-year deal, the club has seemingly finished shopping for first baseman, their position of greatest need outside of pitching when the offseason began. The team looks poised to employ a platoon at first for the 2027 season. Before diving further into the position, let’s look at how we got here. The Mets entered the offseason looking to improve at first base, or at least fortify the position, while most of their remaining position player needs were mostly met. New York has been linked to a few players, most notably Ty France and Alec Bohm, but both players required multi-year commitments, and with France coming off a career year, he was very likely to cash in beyond what the Mets felt comfortable paying him. The Mets were previously interested in Teruaki Sato, who is not a first baseman by trade but would very likely have shifted across the infield had he signed here. With Sato signing a six-year deal with the Cubs, that option is now off the table. That brings us to where we are now. After letting Pete Alonso leave for Baltimore last offseason, the Mets decided to replace him with Jorge Polanco, who had never previously played first but profiled as someone who could manage the position and who was coming off his best season by wRC+ (132) and his third-best by fWAR (2.6). I don’t really need to recount how poorly his first season in Queens went, but let’s just say it was an unmitigated disaster and leave it at that. On the positive side, Jared Young really blossomed in his age-30 season and proved to be a great stop-gap at the position, so much so that he worked his way into the team’s plans for 2027. Entering the offseason, the team had, theoretically, three first basemen on the roster—Young, Polanco, and Mark Vientos, who was tendered a contract prior to the deadline. The rest of their infield appears locked in, with Bo Bichette manning third after exercising his player option, Marcus Semien under contract for two more years, and Francisco Lindor still holding down the short stop position for New York after an injury-plagued and down year. So how do the Mets handle first base in 2027? Well, as mentioned, the Goldschmidt signing all but confirms that the team will employ a lefty-righty platoon, and they seem to have the right guys to do it. Goldschmidt mashed against left-handed pitchers last year, hitting .299/.393/.573 with a 168 wRC+ in 157 at-bats (for comparison, he hit .213/.239/.351 with a 60 wRC+ in 188 at-bats against righties). Young, meanwhile, excelled against righties, slashing .275/.339/.454 with a 120 wRC+ in 251 at-bats (when facing righties, he hit .228/.290/.316 with a 72 wRC+. They were also both solid defensively, with both Young and Goldschmidt finishing 2026 with 2 DRS at first. If the Mets can employ them the way they intend to, the Mets could have a really good pairing at first going into next season. So where does that leave Vientos and Polanco? Let’s start with Vientos. Even though he was tendered a contract, it’s very possible he gets traded before the season begins. He was not a good defender at first base and he hadn’t hit much since his breakout 2024 season, so he really doesn’t have much of a role on the team. If he sticks around, he would, at best, be a DH that would only face left-handers, but using up a valuable roster spot on a player with little versatility and not much of a bat would not be an ideal use of resources. Polanco, on the other hand, will almost certainly be on the roster on Opening Day, since the team is on the hook for $20 million in the final year of his contract. Beyond being ineffective last year, he struggled with injuries and only appeared in 37 games. The Mets’ website doesn’t even list him as a first baseman, instead listing him in the Designated Hitter category on the roster page. After the Goldschmidt signing, it makes sense that Polanco will spend more time as DH than as a first baseman. Polanco could always serve as their emergency first baseman (after all, there are always injuries to account for) and may see sporadic time at other infield spots. For the record, the switch-hitting Polanco has a 114 wRC+ against right-handers and a 97 wRC+ against left-handers. The Mets’ first base plans aren’t without their potential drawbacks. Goldschmidt, for one, is entering his age-39 season and is a risk to regress given his age. Young, who enjoyed a career year at 30, has never really enjoyed any major league success before last year, so it’s hard to evaluate whether he’s a flash-in-the-pan or someone the team can comfortably rely on. Young’s season also ended with a gruesome collision with Nolan McLean that resulted in his a concussion and various lingering injuries. The hope is that he will be fully recovered, but it was a scary moment and it’s hard to know how those injuries will affect him in 2027 and beyond. Despite that, the Mets seem to have a sound plan for first. As long as Goldschmidt doesn’t see much playing time against righties, and Young isn’t played much against lefties, and if Polanco can remain healthy and get back to how he hit prior to 2026, the Mets should get more offensive production at first than they did last year.

title: Thursday Rockpile: The worst case scenario in the Rockies latest trade is… not that bad
summary: What’s the worst that could happen?
content: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - MAY 28: Davis Martin #65 of the Chicago White Sox celebrates against the Minnesota Twins at Rate Field on May 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming into the offseason, two things were clear about the Rockies: They had a desperate organization wide need for pitching . They had 2027 payroll space available . Over the past week the Rockies have been very busy leveraging that payroll space in order to address their pitching needs. Yesterday, Thomas Harding reported that the Rockies have signed LHP David Peterson to a two-year, $32 million dollar deal. Not long after, Jeff Passan reported that they had also signed LHP Patrick Sandoval to a three-year $42 million dollar deal. Look for more on those signings in the coming days. But for now, take a moment to consider the move the Rockies made last week when they began addressing that need for pitching by spending some of their 2027 money in an unusual way: making a trade with the Chicago White Sox for Davis Martin and Luis Castillo . It’s a fascinating trade that saw the Rockies take on the entirety of the $22.75 million owed to Castillo in 2027 in order to get four years of Martin. For the White Sox, this deal made sense because they needed to maximize every dollar spent this year with their limited budget and playoff aspirations. The Rockies, however, do not have that financial pressure in 2027 and used that difference as leverage to gain talent for, essentially, just money. Having had some time to reflect on the deal, however, I think the most interesting aspect is how the worst-case scenario for this trade just isn’t meaningfully bad for the Rockies. By far the largest cost the Rockies paid in this trade is taking on Castillo’s contract. The majority of the baseball world has written off Castillo after his abysmal 2026 performance. That’s understandable given how his underlying data had been trending slowly downward for the past few seasons before falling off a cliff last year. The narrative is obvious: Castillo has simultaneously seen his fastballs lose velocity and his breaking balls lose spin, but some of the effect of this decline was masked by his transition from a very hitter-friendly home venue (Great American Ballpark in Cincinnati) to the most pitcher-friendly home venue in MLB (T-Mobile Park in Seattle) in 2022. This past season, the slow decline reached a breaking point when mixed with ongoing shoulder issues and a move to a less pitcher-friendly home ballpark in Chicago. That multi-year trend in the wrong direction made the bottom falling out in terms of Castillo’s topline results last season seem less like an outlier season in an otherwise stellar career and more like the end of one. Given all of that, it is understandable why both the Mariners and the White Sox were so desperate to stop paying Castillo the money he is owed (and earned with his early career performance). Why, then, should the Rockies be willing to pay Castillo? I’d argue there are a host of reasons that explains their thinking. If Castillo bounces back at all , the Rockies reputation for coaching pitchers will skyrocket . Adding Castillo’s famous name to the Rockies recent success with Antonio Senzatela and Jordan Romano would allow them to become a more palatable destination for free-agent pitchers. Additionally, if Castillo bounces back, the Rockies will be able to flip him at the trade deadline and can afford to pay his salary to increase whatever prospect return is on offer. If Castillo doesn’t bounce back, the Rockies can cut him without anyone blaming it on their inability to coach pitchers. They’ll say he was doomed from the start, and the Rockies made the trade just to get Martin. Essentially, what happens with Castillo is either a non-factor or a net benefit for the Rockies. There’s no real outcome for Castillo that has any meaningfully negative effects on the organization beyond his 2027 salary. Given how little they gave up, other than taking on that salary, any positive results from Castillo himself are purely a cherry on top. Martin, on the other hand, carries the weight of being the centerpiece of the deal. On paper, he is currently in the running to be the Rockies best starting pitcher at the start of the 2027 season . That’s a designation more indicative of how bad the Rockies rotation situation was/is than about Martin’s talent, but it is a designation that bears some weight regardless of fairness. The thing is, Martin is under team control for four seasons, and none of them is guaranteed . The Rockies have him for years if he performs well but can easily non-tender him in the unfortunate scenario where his second half struggles from 2026 persist. The risk with signing a free agent is that the payroll space committed to them is locked in. Underperformance or injuries do not make a difference: Their contracts are guaranteed. The Rockies other two starting pitcher additions this week, Peterson and Sandoval, carry with them the risk of impacting the teams payroll for multiple years even if they aren’t able to transition to Coors Field. Martin’s contract status, on the other hand, comes with full flexibility for the Rockies. Normally, the added cost of adding players that are pre-free agency like Martin comes in the form of the talent needed to acquire them. In this case, the Rockies did not need to give up any prospect that was in their plans moving forward. What’s more, whereas the White Sox couldn’t get an equivalent talent return for Martin because they wanted to get out from under Castillo’s contract, the Rockies do not need to think of the two players as paired together moving forward. If Martin does pitch well, they can easily trade him again for real talent regardless of what happens with Castillo. Essentially, the addition of Martin is all reward with no risk. View Link In the end, the only potentially impactful thing that the Rockies gave up in this deal is the opportunity cost of what else they could have instead spent $22 million in 2027 payroll space on. Neither of the players they sent back to the White Sox are more than a lottery ticket. The additions of Martin and Castillo do not block the playing time of prospects ready for the big leagues. Neither of them come with a big-money long-term commitment that will limit future moves when the team is closer to contention. The worst-case scenario for this trade is that neither Castillo nor Martin are able to pitch better than the revolving door of back of the rotation veterans the Rockies have employed till fill their rotation for the past half decade. They’ll have spent a good chunk of their 2027 payroll to find that out and then be left off in the same situation next year. That’s it. That’s the worst possible outcome of a deal that could plausibly have netted the Rockies four years of a dependable starter and, possibly, a further influx of talent if they are able to help Castillo bounce back and flip him at the deadline. This is a can’t lose situation for the Rockies . . . other than actual baseball games as they are still likely to lose a lot of those in 2027. Join the conversation! title: Five UFC/MMA things to be thankful for in 2026
summary: Happy Thanksgiving, Maniacs! We hope your holiday includes good food, good company, and absolutely no arguments over who really won the main event. It’s been a memorable year for mixed martial arts (MMA). The UFC moved away from pay-per-view (PPV), turned the White House into a fight venue, gave us a revamped Meta APEX, and […]
content: WASHINGTON, DC - JUNE 14: Justin Gaethje strikes Ilia Topuria of Spain in the UFC lightweight championship fight during the UFC Freedom 250 event on the South Lawn at the White House on June 14, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC) Happy Thanksgiving, Maniacs! We hope your holiday includes good food, good company, and absolutely no arguments over who really won the main event. It’s been a memorable year for mixed martial arts (MMA). The UFC moved away from pay-per-view (PPV), turned the White House into a fight venue, gave us a revamped Meta APEX, and watched Justin Gaethje finally capture undisputed gold. And then there’s Josh Hokit , who made sure nobody could accuse 2026 of being boring . Plus, we got two more UFC fight cards left ( schedule here ), Professional Fighters League (PFL) has a couple of cards, and RIZIN will also have its huge New Year’s Eve event. Here are five UFC/MMA things I’m thankful for this year — plus one bonus item that has nothing to do with fighting. NO MORE PPVS! The UFC’s move to Paramount+ means fans in the U.S. no longer have to buy numbered events one at a time . UFC PPV is gone, with the promotion’s full slate of events included with a Paramount+ subscription. A select number of events will also simulcast on CBS in the coming years. That’s a pretty big deal for fight fans who spent years deciding whether a card was worth another PPV ta g. Now, you can watch the big championship fights and the Fight Nights without paying an extra fee every time. The new setup isn’t perfect — subscriptions still cost money , and the UFC is still putting on a lot of events — but it’s easier to follow the sport when the biggest cards aren’t locked behind another purchase. My wallet is thankful. UFC White House No matter where you fall politically, it’s hard to deny that UFC Freedom 250 was a classic. The June 14 event put the Octagon on the White House South Lawn, and every fight ended in a stoppage. All seven bouts finished by knockout or technical knockout ( watch them here ). The spectacle was impossible to ignore: an event staged at one of the most recognizable addresses in the world, with the fights delivering from start to finish . Even if you came for the novelty of seeing the UFC at the White House, there was no shortage of action once the cage door closed. And, of course, the card gave us an unforgettable ending: Gaethje knocking off Ilia Topuria to win the undisputed lightweight title . Josh Hokit Yes, Hokit is cringe . He’s not going to be everybody’s cup of tea , and that’s part of the package. But he’s also delivered two of the year’s best fights, including a wild battle with Curtis Blaydes and his UFC Heavyweight title loss to Ciryl Gane at UFC 334 ( watch highlights ). Hokit brings a kind of over-the-top, corny energy that MMA could use more of. He’s loud, theatrical, and completely committed to the bit — and then he goes out and makes the fights entertaining. You don’t have to love the personality to appreciate the moments he’s created . In a sport where every fighter can start to sound the same in interviews, a little fresh air is welcome. Even if that air is delivered with a catchphrase and a wink. A Revamped Apex For years, the UFC APEX could feel more like a TV set than a live event. The r evamped Meta APEX has helped change that . The facility added more seating, expanded its event floor, improved concessions and gathering spaces, and opened the door for more fans to attend in person . That matters because the atmosphere is part of the show. A bigger crowd gives fighters more energy to feed off and makes the broadcast feel less like a closed-door production. It’s still a smaller venue, but the changes make it feel more like a place fans can go to watch fights — which is a welcome upgrade. Justin Gaethje finally wins UFC gold Gaethje’s road to the undisputed lightweight championship had plenty of heartbreak. He came up short in two previous title fights, then got knocked out by Max Holloway in one of the most unforgettable moments in UFC history . Two years later, he was back on top. Gaethje first handed Paddy Pimblett his first UFC loss ( watch highlights ), then stunned Topuria as a major underdog at the White House to finally become undisputed champion. It was an absurdly good ending to a career spent taking the hardest fights and making them must-watch. There have been more dominant champions and longer title reigns. But few fighters have been as reliably thrilling as Gaethje . Seeing him finally get the belt — on that stage, against that opponent — felt like the kind of story MMA rarely gives us. BONUS: GTA 6 is finally here. I know this has nothing to do with MMA, but Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrived on Nov. 19. After years of waiting, delays, and wondering whether we’d ever make it back to Vice City, the game is out. For that, I am also thankful. I’m about 40 hours in, and I’m completely obsessed with it. Happy Thanksgiving, Maniacs. Here’s hoping 2027 gives us just as much to be thankful for — and maybe a few fewer reasons to check our bank statements after fight night.
